curriculum_source: CFA Program 2027 Level III, Volume 4 (Derivatives and Risk Management), Learning Module 2: Swaps, Forwards, and Futures Strategies

drills.los_text: demonstrate how interest rate swaps, forwards, and futures can be used to modify a portfolio's risk and return

questions.stem: An interest rate swap is best described as:

options.A: an over-the-counter contract exchanging fixed for floating cash flows.
options.B: an exchange-traded contract standardized by a clearinghouse.
options.C: a contract exchanging notional principal at initiation and maturity.

rationales.A: An interest rate swap is an over-the-counter contract between two parties that agree to exchange cash flows on specified payment dates — one based on a variable (floating) interest rate and the other based on a fixed rate, the swap rate, determined at the time the swap is initiated. The swap tenor is when the swap is agreed to expire. Both interest rates are applied to the swap's notional value to determine the size of each payment. Normally the resulting two payments, one fixed and one floating, are in the same currency but will not be equal, so they are typically netted, with the party owing the greater amount paying the difference to the other party. In this manner a party that currently has a fixed (floating) rate obligation or exposure can effectively convert it into a floating (fixed) one.
rationales.B: The swap is a bilateral over-the-counter contract, not an exchange-traded instrument standardized by a futures clearinghouse. Customization of tenor, notional value, payment dates, and reference rate is its hallmark, and that flexibility is exactly what an exchange-standardized contract gives up.
rationales.C: In a single-currency interest rate swap the notional value is not exchanged at initiation or at maturity. It serves only as the base to which the fixed rate and the floating reference rate are applied in sizing each payment; what changes hands is the netted difference between the two interest payments.

questions.stem: A firm has sold £20 million of three-year floating-rate bonds paying a semiannual coupon of the six-month reference rate plus 50 bps. To fix its all-in borrowing cost, the firm is most likely to:

options.A: pay fixed and receive floating on a three-year swap.
options.B: leave the floating-rate exposure unhedged for three years.
options.C: receive fixed and pay floating on a three-year swap.

rationales.A: The firm enters an interest rate swap with a tenor of approximately three years and semiannual payments, paying a fixed par swap rate of 1.25% and receiving the six-month reference rate, so that the swap's floating receipt offsets the floating coupon on the bonds. At the first settlement date, with the six-month reference rate at 0.75%, the firm receives 0.75% × £20 million × (180/360) = £75,000 and pays 1.25% × £20 million × (180/360) = £125,000, a net payment of £50,000 to the swap dealer. The semiannual coupon on the securities is (0.75% + 0.50%) × £20 million × (180/360) = £125,000, so the total payment on the securities and the swap is £175,000. If the reference rate rises to 1.50% at the second settlement date, the bond coupon becomes (1.50% + 0.50%) × £20 million × (180/360) = £200,000 while the firm now receives £25,000 net on the swap, leaving the total payment at £175,000 again. Floating-rate debt combined with a pay-fixed swap has effectively fixed the all-in borrowing cost at the swap rate plus the 50 bp spread.
rationales.B: Leaving the exposure unhedged leaves the all-in cost floating: every semiannual coupon resets with the six-month reference rate, so the £175,000 total of the hedged case would instead rise from £125,000 to £200,000 as the reference rate moved from 0.75% to 1.50%. The pay-fixed swap is what converts that variable cost into a known fixed one over the full three years.
rationales.C: The direction is reversed. A receive-fixed, pay-floating swap adds floating-rate exposure on top of floating-rate debt rather than offsetting it, leaving the firm doubly exposed to a rise in the reference rate. Synthesizing fixed-rate funding out of floating-rate debt requires paying the fixed rate and receiving the floating rate, so that the floating receipt cancels the floating coupon and only the fixed swap rate plus the credit spread remains.

questions.stem: From the perspective of the fixed-rate payer, the modified duration of a pay-fixed, receive-floating interest rate swap is most likely:

options.A: positive and equal to that of the equivalent fixed-rate bond.
options.B: zero.
options.C: negative, the floating-rate bond duration less the fixed-rate bond duration.

rationales.A: The pay-fixed party does not hold the duration of the equivalent fixed-rate bond. It holds the modified duration of the equivalent floating-rate bond minus the modified duration of the equivalent fixed-rate bond, and because the fixed-rate bond duration is positive and the larger of the two, the net figure is negative rather than positive. That negative sign is why the position benefits from rising interest rates instead of losing value as a long fixed-rate bond position would.
rationales.B: The two legs do not offset each other exactly. The equivalent fixed-rate bond carries a positive modified duration that is substantially larger than the near-zero duration of the equivalent floating-rate bond, so the net is not zero: it is negative from the perspective of the fixed-rate payer and positive from the perspective of the fixed-rate receiver.
rationales.C: The modified duration of a swap is the net of the modified durations of the equivalent positions in fixed- and floating-rate bonds, where those bonds have cash flows equivalent to the corresponding cash flows of the swap. The position of the pay-fixed party therefore has the modified duration of a floating-rate bond minus the modified duration of a fixed-rate bond. Because the duration of a fixed-rate bond is positive and larger than the duration of a floating-rate bond, which is near zero, a pay-fixed, receive-floating swap has a negative duration from the perspective of the fixed-rate payer and a positive duration from the perspective of the receiver. That sign makes sense, in that the pay-fixed position would be expected to benefit from rising interest rates.

questions.stem: The swap notional principal that moves a bond portfolio to a target modified duration is most likely the portfolio's market value multiplied by:

options.A: the product of the target and portfolio durations, divided by the swap's duration.
options.B: the swap's duration, divided by the gap between target and portfolio duration.
options.C: the gap between target and portfolio duration, divided by the swap's duration.

rationales.A: The numerator is the duration gap — the target modified duration minus the portfolio's current modified duration — not the product of the two durations. The relationship follows from requiring (MV_P)(MDUR_P) + (N_S)(MDUR_S) = (MV_P)(MDUR_T), which gives N_S = [(MDUR_T − MDUR_P)/MDUR_S](MV_P). A product of the two durations has no basis in that identity, and it would not fall to zero when the portfolio already sits at its target duration and no swap is needed.
rationales.B: The ratio is inverted. The swap's modified duration divides the duration gap rather than being divided by it: N_S = [(MDUR_T − MDUR_P)/MDUR_S](MV_P). Inverting the two terms makes the required notional shrink as the needed change in duration grows and blow up as the gap narrows, the opposite of the correct relationship.
rationales.C: By properly choosing the notional value and the tenor of the swap, the portfolio manager can achieve a combination of the existing portfolio and the interest rate swap that sets overall portfolio duration to the target duration: (MV_P)(MDUR_P) + (N_S)(MDUR_S) = (MV_P)(MDUR_T). The equivalence ΔP = (N_S)(ΔS) becomes (MV_P)(MDUR_T − MDUR_P) = (N_S)(MDUR_S), so the swap notional principal is N_S = [(MDUR_T − MDUR_P)/MDUR_S](MV_P), where MDUR_T is the target modified duration, MDUR_P is the portfolio's modified duration, MDUR_S is the swap's modified duration, and MV_P is the market value of the bond portfolio.

questions.stem: A manager holding €50 million of fixed-rate bonds with an average modified duration of 5.5 wants to lower portfolio modified duration to 4.5 using a two-year interest rate swap whose modified duration is −2.00 to the fixed-rate payer. The swap position is most likely:

options.A: €25 million notional, receiving fixed and paying floating.
options.B: €9.1 million notional, paying fixed and receiving floating.
options.C: €25 million notional, paying fixed and receiving floating.

rationales.A: The notional is right but the direction is backwards. Reducing modified duration requires adding a negative-duration position, which means paying the fixed rate and receiving the floating rate. Receiving fixed and paying floating adds a positive-duration position and would push the portfolio's modified duration above 5.5 rather than down to the 4.5 target, so the €25 million notional is correct only in the pay-fixed direction.
rationales.B: The denominator is the swap's modified duration from the fixed-rate payer's perspective, −2.00, not the portfolio's own modified duration of 5.5. The calculation is N_S = [(4.50 − 5.50)/(−2.00)] × €50,000,000 = €25,000,000, not roughly €9.1 million; substituting the portfolio's duration for the swap's understates the notional needed by more than half and would leave the portfolio well short of its target duration.
rationales.C: The manager wants to reduce modified duration from 5.5 to 4.5 without selling any of the securities, so he adds a negative-duration position by entering an interest rate swap as the fixed-rate payer and floating-rate receiver. With the two-year swap's estimated modified duration at −2.00 from the perspective of the fixed-rate payer, N_S = [(MDUR_T − MDUR_P)/MDUR_S](MV_P) = [(4.50 − 5.50)/(−2.00)] × €50,000,000 = €25,000,000. A €25 million pay-fixed, receive-floating position therefore brings the portfolio's modified duration to the 4.5 target.

questions.stem: An investor who hedges a bond portfolio with an interest rate swap is most likely to:

options.A: retain basis risk from imperfect substitution.
options.B: face basis risk only on counterparty default.
options.C: eliminate basis risk entirely.

rationales.A: Most of the time the hedging instrument and the asset or portfolio to be hedged are imperfect substitutes. The market risk this leaves behind is called basis risk, or spread risk: the difference between the market performance of the asset and that of the derivative instrument used to hedge it. When an interest rate swap is used as the hedge, changes in the underlying reference rate of the derivative contract, and therefore in the value of the swap, need not perfectly mirror changes in the value of the bond portfolio. The composition of the bond portfolio can also bear market risks other than interest rate risk: a portfolio of corporate bonds hedged with an interest rate swap still leaves the investor exposed to credit spread risk even after interest rate risk has been hedged.
rationales.B: This conflates basis risk, or spread risk, with counterparty credit risk. Basis risk arises from the imperfect co-movement of the hedged asset and the hedge, and it is present even with a counterparty that never defaults. Counterparty default risk on an over-the-counter swap is a distinct exposure, addressed by collateral, daily marking to market and central clearing, none of which removes the spread between the performance of the portfolio and the performance of the swap.
rationales.C: The swap and the bond portfolio are imperfect substitutes, so the value of the swap does not move one-for-one with the value of the portfolio. Putting the swap on converts interest rate exposure but leaves residual basis, or spread, risk: the underlying reference rate of the swap and the yields driving the portfolio can move apart, and a corporate bond portfolio retains credit spread risk once its interest rate risk has been hedged.

questions.stem: A forward rate agreement (FRA) is most likely:

options.A: an instrument settled by exchanging the full notional amount.
options.B: an exchange-traded contract on physical bond delivery.
options.C: an over-the-counter hedge against future borrowing rates.

rationales.A: Only the discounted interest difference settles. An FRA pays the discounted difference between the interest rate agreed on in the contract and the rate actually prevailing at the time of settlement, applied to the notional amount of the contract. The notional itself never changes hands, which is why the credit exposure created by an FRA is a small fraction of the notional on which its payment is calculated.
rationales.B: An FRA is an over-the-counter contract, negotiated bilaterally and cash settled on an interest rate; it hedges an expected borrowing or a general exposure to the future level of rates. A standardized, clearinghouse-guaranteed contract calling for physical delivery of government bonds describes a bond futures contract instead, and such a contract settles on a bond price rather than on a reference rate.
rationales.C: A forward rate agreement is an over-the-counter derivative instrument used mainly to hedge a loan expected to be taken out in the near future, or to hedge against changes in the level of interest rates in the future. With advanced settled at maturity, the FRA will settle only the discounted difference between the interest rate agreed on in the contract and the actual rate prevailing at the time of settlement, applied on the notional amount of the contract.

questions.stem: Compared with interest rate futures, forward contracts are most likely:

options.A: identical in every practical respect.
options.B: customizable, but exposed to counterparty risk.
options.C: guaranteed by a central clearinghouse.

rationales.A: The difference in venue is substantive rather than cosmetic, and it is what drives the choice between the two. A forward is negotiated over the counter, so notional, maturity and reference rate can be tailored, but the investor takes on counterparty risk. A futures contract is standardized and guaranteed by a clearinghouse, so counterparty risk is virtually zero but the terms are fixed by the exchange.
rationales.B: Forwards, like swaps, are over-the-counter instruments and are especially useful because they can be customized, but they do have counterparty risk. In contrast, exchange-traded interest rate futures contracts are standardized and guaranteed by a clearinghouse, so counterparty risk is virtually zero. Regulatory changes in global markets are moving both over-the-counter swaps and forward contracts toward a clearing process as well. Clearing reduces the risk that one counterparty will default on its obligations, by requiring collateral for trades and by daily marking to market of open positions, so that the counterparty risk associated with any single cleared trade is virtually zero. Even so, there remains the risk that a major counterparty will fail to carry out its obligations, as Lehman Brothers did, causing operational risks for investors.
rationales.C: The credit arrangement runs the other way. It is the exchange-traded futures contract that is guaranteed by the clearinghouse, with collateral and daily marking to market, so its counterparty risk is virtually zero. The over-the-counter forward bears counterparty risk, which the investor accepts in exchange for the ability to customize the terms of the contract.

questions.stem: A bond portfolio fully hedged with an interest rate swap is most likely:

options.A: immunized against changes in yields.
options.B: guaranteed to grow at the fixed swap rate.
options.C: immunized only if its duration matches the longest liability.

rationales.A: When a bond portfolio is fully hedged, its value is immunized with respect to changes in yields. This can be stated as ΔP = Ns × ΔS, where ΔP is the change in the value of the bond portfolio and ΔS is the change in the value of the swap for a given change in interest rates; the notional principal of the swap is then determined as Ns = ΔP/ΔS. To reduce changes in the value of a fixed-rate portfolio, the manager will want to lower the overall duration by exchanging part of the fixed-rate income stream for a floating-rate stream, which is done by entering an interest rate swap in which the portfolio manager pays the fixed rate and receives the floating rate.
rationales.B: Full hedging immunizes the value of the portfolio against changes in yields: the change in the value of the swap offsets the change in the value of the portfolio, so that ΔP − Ns × ΔS is approximately zero for a given move in rates. That is a statement about price sensitivity, not about return. It does not convert the portfolio into an instrument that compounds at the fixed swap rate, because the realized return still depends on the portfolio's own coupons and on the floating rate received under the swap.
rationales.C: Immunization here means neutralizing the value of the portfolio with respect to yields, and the swap used to do it is a pay-fixed, receive-floating swap, which lowers the portfolio's duration rather than lengthening it. Matching the duration of assets to the horizon of a long liability is a different application of immunization; it is not what is accomplished by fully hedging a fixed-rate bond portfolio with an interest rate swap.

questions.stem: To hedge portfolio duration with bond futures, the basis point value (BPV) hedge ratio is most likely:

options.A: portfolio BPV less target BPV, divided by cheapest-to-deliver BPV over the conversion factor.
options.B: target BPV less portfolio BPV, divided by cheapest-to-deliver BPV times the conversion factor.
options.C: target BPV less portfolio BPV, divided by cheapest-to-deliver BPV over the conversion factor.

rationales.A: The numerator is the target basis point value less the portfolio basis point value, BPV_T − BPV_P. Taking the portfolio figure first reverses the sign of the hedge ratio and therefore the direction of the futures position, so a hedge intended to shorten duration would be implemented as a long position and would lengthen it instead.
rationales.B: The basis point value of the futures contract is the cheapest-to-deliver bond's basis point value divided by the conversion factor, BPV_F ≈ BPV_CTD/CF, not multiplied by it. Because a conversion factor is typically less than one, multiplying understates BPV_F and so overstates the number of contracts the hedge requires.
rationales.C: BPV_HR = (BPV_T − BPV_P)/BPV_F, where the futures basis point value is approximated as BPV_F ≈ BPV_CTD/CF. Substituting gives the more general form BPV_HR = [(BPV_T − BPV_P)/BPV_CTD] × CF, in which BPV_T is the target basis point value, BPV_P is the portfolio basis point value, BPV_CTD is the basis point value of the cheapest-to-deliver bond, and CF is its conversion factor. The expression follows from the hedging condition BPV_P + BPV_HR × BPV_F = BPV_T, which sets the hedged portfolio's basis point value equal to the target.

questions.stem: The cheapest-to-deliver bond for a Euro-Bund futures contract has a modified duration of 8.623, a price of 98.14 per 100 of par and a conversion factor of 0.619489, and the contract size is €100,000. The basis point value of that bond is closest to:

rationales.A: €52.43 multiplies the bond's basis point value by the conversion factor: €84.63 × 0.619489. The conversion factor is applied later, in the futures hedge ratio, where the futures basis point value is approximated as BPV_F ≈ BPV_CTD/CF. It plays no part in computing the cheapest-to-deliver bond's own basis point value, which is €84.63.
rationales.B: BPV_CTD = MDUR_CTD × 0.0001 × [(price/100) × contract size] = 8.623 × 0.0001 × [(98.14/100) × €100,000] = €84.63. The market value underlying one contract is (98.14/100) × €100,000 = €98,140, and one basis point of yield moves that value by about €84.63. This figure is then combined with the conversion factor of 0.619489 in the futures hedge ratio calculation.
rationales.C: €86.23 applies the modified duration to the full €100,000 par amount. Basis point value must be based on the market value of the bond position, (98.14/100) × €100,000 = €98,140, which gives 8.623 × 0.0001 × €98,140 = €84.63. Using par overstates the exposure whenever the bond trades below 100.

questions.stem: A manager uses Euro-Bund futures to lower the modified duration of a €49,531,000 bond portfolio from 9.50 to 8.50. For this hedge, it is most likely that:

options.A: the manager buys 36 Euro-Bund futures contracts.
options.B: the portfolio basis point value is €47,054.45.
options.C: the portfolio basis point value is €42,101.35.

rationales.A: The sign is reversed. With BPV_P = €47,054.45 and BPV_T = €42,101.35, the number of contracts is [(€42,101.35 − €47,054.45)/€84.63] × 0.619489 = −36.26, or roughly 36 contracts short, using a cheapest-to-deliver basis point value of €84.63 and a conversion factor of 0.619489. A negative hedge ratio means the manager must sell Euro-Bund futures to reduce the portfolio's modified duration from 9.50 to 8.50; buying futures would add duration and move the portfolio away from the target.
rationales.B: BPV_P = 9.50 × 0.0001 × €49,531,000 = €47,054.45, and the portfolio's target basis point value is BPV_T = 8.50 × 0.0001 × €49,531,000 = €42,101.35. To achieve the target modified duration of 8.50 the manager implements a short position in Euro-Bund futures: with the same cheapest-to-deliver bond, whose basis point value is €84.63, and a conversion factor of 0.619489, the number of futures is [(€42,101.35 − €47,054.45)/€84.63] × 0.619489 = −36.26, so about 36 contracts are sold. The portfolio basis point value is sometimes printed as €47,054.50, a rounding artifact; the exact product is €47,054.45, and the hedge count of −36.26, or sell 36, is unchanged either way.
rationales.C: €42,101.35 applies the target modified duration of 8.50 to the portfolio's value, so it is the target basis point value, BPV_T, not the current one. The portfolio's own basis point value uses its existing modified duration of 9.50: BPV_P = 9.50 × 0.0001 × €49,531,000 = €47,054.45. Confusing the two collapses the numerator of the hedge ratio to zero and implies no futures position is needed.

questions.stem: In practice, a duration hedge implemented with bond futures is most likely:

options.A: limited in accuracy only by broker commissions.
options.B: exact, with no residual basis or duration error.
options.C: inexact, because the cheapest-to-deliver bond can change.

rationales.A: Commissions are trivial next to the structural sources of hedging error. The hedge is placed using the cheapest-to-deliver bond, and that bond can switch over the holding period, changing the duration of the futures contract; convexity makes the relationship between interest rates and bond prices non-linear; and the term structure often shifts in non-parallel ways. A hedge executed at zero commission would still leave residual basis and duration error.
rationales.B: A futures hedge is not exact in practice. The hedge is done with the cheapest-to-deliver bond, whose identity can change over the holding period, so the duration of the futures contract can change with it; the relationship between interest rates and bond prices is not linear, owing to convexity, so a basis point value computed at today's yield level misstates the response to a large move; and the term structure of interest rates often changes via non-parallel moves, so a single duration figure cannot capture the portfolio's response. Each of these leaves residual basis and duration error.
rationales.C: In the real world the hedging results are imperfect because the hedge is done with the cheapest-to-deliver bond, and since the cheapest-to-deliver bond can change over the holding period, the duration of the futures contract can also change. Two further sources of error compound this: the relationship between interest rates and bond prices is not linear, owing to convexity, and the term structure of interest rates often changes via non-parallel moves rather than by a uniform shift in yields.

drills.los_text: demonstrate how currency swaps, forwards, and futures can be used to modify a portfolio's risk and return

questions.stem: Compared with an interest rate swap, a currency swap is most likely:

options.A: based on interest rates in different currencies.
options.B: identical in structure and cash flows.
options.C: structured without any exchange of principal.

rationales.A: A currency swap is similar to an interest rate swap, but it is different in two ways: the interest rates are associated with different currencies, and the notional principal amounts may or may not be exchanged at the beginning and end of the swap's life. Currency swaps help the parties in the swap to hedge against the risk of exchange rate fluctuations and to achieve better rate outcomes. Although an exchange of notional principals often occurs, the parties may agree not to do this: some types of hedge transactions are designed to hedge only foreign interest cash flows and not principal payments, so a principal exchange on a currency swap would not be necessary.
rationales.B: The two are not identical. A currency swap's interest rates are associated with different currencies, whereas an interest rate swap exchanges fixed for floating payments within a single currency, and a currency swap's notional principal amounts are typically exchanged at the beginning and at the end of its life. Those two features are precisely what distinguish the currency swap, and they also give it exchange rate exposure that a single-currency swap does not have.
rationales.C: An exchange of notional principals at the beginning and end of the swap's life is one of the two features that distinguish a currency swap, and it is the usual arrangement. The parties may agree to omit it, for instance when a hedge is designed to cover only foreign interest cash flows and not principal payments, but that is an exception rather than the rule, so saying principal is never exchanged is too strong.

questions.stem: A cross-currency basis swap is most likely:

options.A: an exchange of fixed payments within a single currency.
options.B: an exchange of notional principals to obtain cheaper funding.
options.C: an exchange of interest only, limiting settlement risk.

rationales.A: Fixed-for-fixed payments within one currency is neither cross-currency nor a basis swap. A cross-currency basis swap periodically sets interest rate payments, mostly floating for floating, separately in two different currencies, and its purpose is to move funding raised in one currency into the currency the borrower actually needs.
rationales.B: A cross-currency basis swap exchanges notional principals because the goal of the transaction is to issue at a more favorable funding rate and swap the amount back to the currency of choice. Firms that need foreign-denominated cash can obtain the funding in their local currency and then swap the local currency for the required foreign currency using a cross-currency basis swap. The swap periodically sets interest rate payments, mostly floating for floating, separately in the two different currencies. The net effect is to use a loan in a local currency to take out a loan in a foreign currency while avoiding any foreign exchange risk, because the exchange rate is fixed.
rationales.C: The notional principals are exchanged rather than avoided, since the purpose of the transaction is to issue at a more favorable funding rate in one currency and swap the proceeds back into the currency of choice. Fixing the exchange rate on that principal exchange is what removes the foreign exchange risk. Settlement and default exposure are managed through collateral and clearing arrangements, not by leaving the principal amounts unexchanged.

questions.stem: A Canadian private equity firm is funding a USD40 million buyout of a US electronics manufacturer. A US dollar loan would cost the semiannual US dollar reference rate plus 100 bps, while the firm can instead borrow CAD50 million for three years at the Canadian dollar reference rate plus 65 bps, with a three-year CAD-USD cross-currency basis swap quoted at -15 bps at USD/CAD 0.8000. The firm's lowest-cost funding approach is most likely to:

options.A: borrow US dollars directly from a US lender.
options.B: borrow Canadian dollars and swap them into US dollars.
options.C: borrow Canadian dollars and hedge with a single-currency interest rate swap.

rationales.A: Borrowing US dollars directly means paying the semiannual US dollar reference rate plus 100 bps, which is precisely the spread the firm is trying to avoid. Funding in the local Canadian market at the Canadian dollar reference rate plus 65 bps and swapping the proceeds at a basis of -15 bps produces an effective spread of 80 bps (= 65 bps + 15 bps), a saving of 20 bps a year on the equivalent of USD40 million of funding.
rationales.B: The firm can borrow more cheaply in its local Canadian market, so it funds the buyout in Canadian dollars: it borrows CAD50 million for three years at the semiannual Canadian dollar reference floating rate plus 65 bps, then asks a New York dealer to quote a three-year cross-currency basis swap with semiannual interest payments to exchange the CAD50 million into US dollars. That swap is quoted at -15 bps at a rate of USD/CAD 0.8000. As the lender of Canadian dollars in the swap, the firm receives the Canadian dollar reference rate, assumed to be 1.95%, minus 15 bps every six months, in exchange for paying the US dollar reference rate on the US dollars it has borrowed. Because it pays the Canadian dollar floating rate plus 65 bps on the bank loan, the effective spread paid becomes 80 bps (= 65 bps + 15 bps), compared with the 100 bps spread it would have paid had it borrowed in US dollars.
rationales.C: The transaction is a floating-for-floating cross-currency basis swap exchanging Canadian dollars for US dollars, not a single-currency fixed-for-fixed interest rate swap. A single-currency swap converts fixed interest into floating interest, or the reverse, within one currency; it would leave the firm holding Canadian dollar proceeds with no US dollars to pay for the acquisition and would do nothing about the mismatch between a Canadian dollar loan and a US dollar asset.

questions.stem: The basis in a cross-currency basis swap is best described as:

options.A: the full interest rate differential between the two currencies.
options.B: a spread quoted on the non-US dollar leg.
options.C: a spread quoted on the US dollar leg.

rationales.A: The basis is the deviation from covered interest rate parity, not the interest rate differential itself. If covered interest rate parity held, a forward exchange rate would be determined by the spot exchange rate and the interest rate differential between foreign and domestic currencies over the term of the forward rate. Parity usually does not hold, and the residual that remains is the basis: the difference between the interest rates in the cross-currency basis swap and those used to determine forward exchange rates. It is typically a handful of basis points, not a whole rate differential.
rationales.B: The basis is quoted on the non-US dollar leg of the swap. Paying the basis would mean borrowing the other currency versus lending US dollars, whereas receiving the basis implies lending the other currency versus borrowing US dollars. The basis itself is the difference between the interest rates in the cross-currency basis swap and those used to determine the forward exchange rates: if covered interest rate parity holds, a forward exchange rate is determined by the spot exchange rate and the interest rate differential between the two currencies over the term of the forward rate; usually covered interest rate parity does not hold, and that deviation gives rise to the basis. A three-year CAD-USD swap quoted at -15 bps, for instance, means the Canadian dollar leg carries the Canadian dollar reference rate minus 15 bps while the US dollar leg carries the US dollar reference rate flat.
rationales.C: By convention the basis is quoted on the non-US dollar leg of the cross-currency swap, never on the US dollar leg, which pays its reference rate flat. A quote of -15 bps on a CAD-USD swap therefore adjusts the Canadian dollar rate downward to the Canadian dollar reference rate minus 15 bps; it does not adjust the US dollar rate.

questions.stem: A Canadian private equity firm borrows CAD50 million and enters a three-year CAD-USD cross-currency basis swap at USD/CAD 0.8000 to fund a USD40 million acquisition in the United States. At the inception of the swap, it is most likely that:

options.A: the firm exchanges no principal.
options.B: the firm delivers US dollars and receives Canadian dollars.
options.C: the firm delivers Canadian dollars and receives US dollars.

rationales.A: Unlike single-currency interest rate swaps, cross-currency swaps typically do exchange notional principal at inception. Here the firm delivers CAD50 million to the swap dealer and receives USD40 million (= CAD50 million x 0.8000 USD/CAD). That exchange is the whole purpose of the structure: it converts cheap Canadian dollar bank borrowing into the US dollars the acquisition requires, at an exchange rate fixed for the life of the swap.
rationales.B: The direction is reversed. The firm needs US dollars for its US acquisition, so at inception it delivers the Canadian dollar notional (N) of CAD50 million and receives US dollars at the agreed rate (N x S0 = CAD50 million x 0.8000 USD/CAD = USD40 million). The firm delivers US dollars and receives Canadian dollars only at maturity, when the principal exchange is reversed and the CAD50 million is used to repay the local lender.
rationales.C: At inception the Canadian private equity firm delivers Canadian dollars (N) in exchange for US dollars (at a rate of N x S0): CAD50 million goes from the firm to the swap dealer, and USD40 million (= CAD50 million x 0.8000 USD/CAD) comes back. The proceeds of the Canadian dollar bank loan are thereby converted into the US dollars needed to fund the buyout, with the exchange rate S0 = USD/CAD 0.8000 agreed at the start and applied to this flow, to every interest payment date and to the re-exchange at maturity.

questions.stem: A Canadian firm's three-year CAD-USD cross-currency basis swap is quoted at -15 bps. On the first settlement date, the Canadian dollar reference rate is 1.95% and the US dollar reference rate is 2.50%. The Canadian dollar rate on the swap is closest to:

rationales.A: The basis is negative, so it is subtracted rather than added: the Canadian dollar rate on the swap is 1.80% (= 1.95% - 15 bps), not 2.10%. Adding the basis would raise the rate the firm receives on the Canadian dollar leg and would turn a funding saving into a funding cost, which is the opposite of what a negative quoted basis does.
rationales.B: This is the unadjusted Canadian dollar reference rate, which would be the swap rate only if the -15 bp basis attached to the US dollar leg. The basis is quoted on the non-US dollar leg of the swap, so in a CAD-USD structure it attaches to the Canadian dollar leg and lowers the rate received there to 1.80% (= 1.95% - 15 bps). The US dollar leg carries its 2.50% reference rate flat, with no basis adjustment.
rationales.C: On the first settlement date the Canadian dollar reference rate is 1.95% and the basis is -15 bps, so the Canadian dollar rate on the swap is 1.80% (= 1.95% - 15 bps), while the US dollar rate is 2.50%. The firm receives CAD50 million x 1.80% x 180/360 = CAD450,000 and pays CAD50 million x 0.8000 USD/CAD x 2.50% x 180/360 = USD500,000. The interest payment on the firm's own bank loan is CAD50 million x (1.95% + 0.65%) x 180/360 = CAD650,000, so after the CAD450,000 received on the swap its net Canadian dollar payment is CAD200,000. At USD/CAD 0.8000 that net payment corresponds to USD160,000, which added to the USD500,000 paid on the swap totals USD660,000. Had the firm taken the US dollar loan instead, it would have paid USD700,000 (= USD40 million x [2.50% + 1.00%] x 180/360) every six months.

questions.stem: A Canadian private equity firm funded a USD40 million buyout by borrowing CAD50 million and swapping the proceeds through a three-year CAD-USD cross-currency basis swap at USD/CAD 0.8000. At the maturity of the swap, it is most likely that:

options.A: the firm returns US dollars and receives Canadian dollars.
options.B: the firm exchanges no further principal.
options.C: the firm keeps the US dollars and pays only accrued interest.

rationales.A: At the maturity of the swap, and after a successful exit from the buyout through a US initial public offering, the firm swaps back US dollars in exchange for Canadian dollars at the rate agreed at the start (USD x 1/S0): it returns USD40 million to the swap dealer and receives CAD50 million (= USD40 million x 1/0.8000), which it uses to pay off its Canadian lender. Because the re-exchange uses the original USD/CAD 0.8000 rather than the spot rate prevailing in three years, the firm bears no exchange rate risk on the principal.
rationales.B: Maturity brings the reverse principal exchange, and that reversal is how the firm unwinds the funding: it returns USD40 million and receives CAD50 million (= USD40 million x 1/0.8000) at the original USD/CAD 0.8000, and only with those Canadian dollars can it repay the CAD50 million bank loan. A cross-currency swap exchanges principal both at inception and at maturity, unlike a single-currency interest rate swap.
rationales.C: Following the initial public offering exit, the firm swaps the US dollars back for Canadian dollars at the original rate S0 of USD/CAD 0.8000, receiving CAD50 million for the USD40 million returned. Keeping the US dollars would leave the CAD50 million bank loan outstanding and would expose the firm to whatever exchange rate prevailed at the time of repayment. Periodic interest payments do end with the final settlement, but the principal re-exchange takes place as well.

questions.stem: Currency risk is best described as the risk that:

options.A: domestic interest rates rise and depress domestic bond prices.
options.B: a foreign currency asset or liability changes in value on conversion into the domestic currency.
options.C: foreign currency assets, but never liabilities, change in value on conversion.

rationales.A: A rise in domestic interest rates that lowers domestic bond prices is interest rate risk, not currency risk. Currency risk concerns the values at which positions convert across currencies, and it arises from exposure to a foreign currency rather than from the level of domestic yields. The two can appear together in one position, but they are distinct exposures and are hedged with different instruments.
rationales.B: Currency risk is the risk that the value of a current or future asset (liability) in a foreign currency will decrease (increase) when converted into the domestic currency. The definition is symmetric: a foreign currency asset loses domestic currency value when the foreign currency depreciates, and a foreign currency liability grows in domestic currency terms when the foreign currency appreciates. It also covers future, not only current, positions. Currency swaps, forwards and futures can all be used to effectively alter these currency risk exposures.
rationales.C: Liabilities carry currency risk symmetrically with assets: a foreign currency liability increases in domestic currency terms when the foreign currency appreciates, just as a foreign currency asset decreases when the foreign currency depreciates. The definition explicitly spans both current and future assets and liabilities, which is why a firm with foreign currency debt hedges that debt exactly as an investor hedges a foreign currency holding.

questions.stem: The exchange rate used for the cash flows of a cross-currency basis swap is best described by the statement that:

options.A: the notional is redenominated at each payment date using current market rates.
options.B: a single rate agreed at the start applies to every payment.
options.C: the prevailing spot rate applies at each settlement date.

rationales.A: The notional and the rate at which it converts are both locked in at the start of the swap, so no redenomination takes place at interim payment dates. For the Canadian firm, the notional principal of the Canadian dollar leg stays at N = CAD50 million and the conversion rate stays at S0 = USD/CAD 0.8000 throughout, which is what makes the schedule of payments known in advance in both currencies.
rationales.B: N is the notional principal of the Canadian dollar leg of the swap, and S0, agreed at the start, is the spot exchange rate for all payments: at inception, on the interest payment dates and at maturity. For the Canadian private equity firm this means N = CAD50 million and S0 = USD/CAD 0.8000, so the same rate converts the initial exchange of CAD50 million for USD40 million, each semiannual interest payment, and the final re-exchange of USD40 million for CAD50 million. Fixing one rate for every cash flow is what removes exchange rate risk on the principal exchange and on the periodic payments.
rationales.C: S0 is fixed at inception and governs all payments on the swap, including the initial exchange, the periodic interest payments and the final re-exchange. Resetting each flow to the prevailing spot rate would reintroduce exactly the currency risk the structure is designed to remove, leaving the firm uncertain how many Canadian dollars its US dollar obligations would cost.

questions.stem: The statement that best describes the relationship between covered interest rate parity, forward exchange rates and the cross-currency basis is that:

options.A: the basis arises because covered interest rate parity holds at all times.
options.B: the forward rate would reflect only spot rates and the interest rate differential if parity held.
options.C: forward rates are set independently of spot rates and interest rate differentials.

rationales.A: The basis exists precisely because covered interest rate parity does not hold. Were parity to hold at all times, the interest rates embedded in a cross-currency basis swap would match those used to determine the forward exchange rate and the basis would be zero. Funding frictions, balance sheet costs and imbalances in the demand for dollar funding leave a residual deviation, and that residual is the basis.
rationales.B: If covered interest rate parity holds, a forward exchange rate is determined by the spot exchange rate and the interest rate differential between foreign and domestic currencies over the term of the forward rate. However, covered interest rate parity usually does not hold, and those deviations give rise to the basis in cross-currency basis swaps. The basis is the difference between the interest rates in the cross-currency basis swap and those used to determine the forward exchange rates, and it is typically not zero, which is why a swap is quoted at a level such as -15 bps on its non-US dollar leg.
rationales.C: Spot rates and interest rate differentials remain the foundation of the forward rate; the basis is only the deviation layered on top of that relationship. Forward rates are not set independently of them, and a forward quote can be decomposed into the parity-implied rate plus the deviation that the cross-currency basis measures.

questions.stem: In a cross-currency basis swap, paying the basis is best described as:

options.A: borrowing the other currency versus lending US dollars.
options.B: exchanging fixed-rate for floating-rate interest in US dollars.
options.C: lending the other currency versus borrowing US dollars.

rationales.A: The basis is quoted on the non-US dollar leg of the swap. Paying the basis means borrowing the other currency versus lending US dollars, whereas receiving the basis implies lending the other currency versus borrowing US dollars. In the Canadian buyout funding structure, a three-year CAD-USD cross-currency swap quoted at -15 bps means the Canadian private equity firm, as the lender of the Canadian dollars in the swap, receives the Canadian dollar reference rate, assumed to be 1.95%, minus 15 bps every six months, in exchange for paying the US dollar reference rate on the US dollars it has borrowed. That firm is therefore receiving, not paying, the basis.
rationales.B: The direction of the basis concerns which currency is being borrowed and which is being lent, not a conversion between fixed-rate and floating-rate interest within a single currency. Swapping fixed for floating in one currency is a plain single-currency interest rate swap, which involves no exchange of currencies and carries no basis at all.
rationales.C: Lending the other currency versus borrowing US dollars is what receiving the basis means. Paying the basis is the opposite side: borrowing the other currency versus lending US dollars. The basis is quoted on the non-US dollar leg, so the side that borrows that currency pays the quoted spread.

questions.stem: Currency risk exposures are most appropriately altered using:

options.A: exchange-traded currency futures only.
options.B: currency swaps only when no principal is exchanged.
options.C: currency swaps, forwards or futures.

rationales.A: Over-the-counter currency swaps and forwards also effectively alter currency risk exposures, so futures are not the only instrument available. Forwards, like swaps, are over-the-counter instruments and are especially useful because they can be customized, although they carry counterparty risk; exchange-traded futures contracts are standardized and guaranteed by a clearinghouse, so counterparty risk is virtually zero. The choice among them is about customization, credit and operational preference, not about which one can transfer currency risk.
rationales.B: Currency swaps typically do exchange notional principal at inception and again at maturity, and they hedge currency risk precisely because of that exchange: the initial exchange delivers the currency needed, and the final re-exchange at the rate agreed at the start removes exchange rate risk on the principal. Principal exchange is therefore a feature of the hedge rather than a barrier to it.
rationales.C: Currency swaps, forwards and futures can all be used to effectively alter currency risk exposures. They differ in mechanics rather than in purpose: forwards, like swaps, are over-the-counter and can be customized but carry counterparty risk, while futures are exchange-traded, standardized and cleared, so counterparty risk is virtually zero. Swaps involve a series of cash flow exchanges over time, whereas forwards settle once at maturity and futures are settled through daily marking to market. Currency swaps may also involve an exchange of principal at the beginning and the end, which forwards and futures typically do not.

questions.stem: For a private investor holding a large, dividend-paying concentrated stock position, a total return swap is most likely to:

options.A: require sale of the position, triggering an immediate capital gains tax.
options.B: transfer the stock's total performance to the counterparty for a prespecified fee.
options.C: increase the holder's exposure to the stock's price movements.

rationales.A: No sale occurs. The swap sheds the economic exposure while title to the shares stays with the investor, so the tax event is deferred rather than triggered, and that deferral is much of the structure's appeal.
rationales.B: An investor holding a large, concentrated position in a company's stock that pays dividends on a regular basis may expect that over the next six months the total return from the stock, including the dividends received, will be negative, and so want to neutralize the long exposure temporarily without selling the shares on an exchange and losing ownership and voting rights. She can enter into a total return swap requiring her to transfer the total performance of the stock, that is, its total return, to the swap counterparty at prespecified dates for an agreed-on fee. Under the terms of the swap she pays the counterparty the share price appreciation plus the dividends received over the life of the contract; if the stock price decreases, she receives the share price depreciation but net of the dividends. At the same prespecified dates, the investor receives from the counterparty an agreed-on floating-rate interest payment based on the swap notional. The long exposure is therefore neutralized temporarily while ownership and voting rights are retained.
rationales.C: The swap neutralizes the exposure rather than increasing it: the total performance of the stock, dividends and price change alike, is paid away in exchange for a floating-rate receipt on the swap notional.

questions.stem: An equity swap whose underlying is a single stock is most likely:

options.A: settled either in cash or physically.
options.B: settled only physically, by delivering the shares at maturity.
options.C: settled only in cash.

rationales.A: Equity swaps that have a single stock as the underlying can be cash settled or physically settled. If the swap is cash settled, on the termination date of the contract the equity swap receiver will receive, or pay, the equity appreciation, or depreciation, in cash. If the swap is physically settled, on the termination date the receiver will receive the quantity of the single stock specified in the contract and pay the notional amount. Both routes are available, so neither method is mandatory.
rationales.B: Physical delivery is not mandatory. The same single-stock equity swap can instead be cash settled, in which case on the termination date the receiver receives or pays the equity appreciation or depreciation in cash and no shares change hands.
rationales.C: Cash settlement is not the only route. Physical settlement is an available alternative: on the termination date the equity swap receiver takes delivery of the quantity of stock specified in the contract and pays the notional amount.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager is the receiver in a six-month equity swap with notional principal of EUR 4.5 million that requires physical settlement, at maturity, of 300,000 shares of the Italian insurer Generali, whose price at maturity is EUR 16. Relative to the same swap under cash settlement, the manager's economic outcome is most likely:

options.A: the same, with shares received in place of a cash difference.
options.B: materially different.
options.C: the same, but reached through interim cash flows.

rationales.A: At maturity of the swap the portfolio manager receives 300,000 shares of Generali and pays EUR 4.5 million, which corresponds to a purchase price per share of EUR 15 (= EUR 4.5 million/300,000); he also pays the interest on the swap based on the agreed-on rate. With Generali at EUR 16, selling the shares received implies a gain of EUR 300,000 (= [EUR 16 - EUR 15] x 300,000). Had the same swap been cash settled instead of physically settled, at maturity the manager would have received EUR 300,000, given by EUR 16, the swap settlement price, less EUR 15, the agreed price on the swap, multiplied by 300,000, against the same payment of interest on the swap. The economics are identical; only the mechanics differ, with shares exchanged for the notional under physical settlement and a net cash difference paid under cash settlement.
rationales.B: The outcome is EUR 300,000 either way: EUR 300,000 of share value above the EUR 15 agreed price under physical settlement, and a EUR 300,000 cash receipt under cash settlement, in each case against the swap interest. Settlement mechanics differ; the economics do not.
rationales.C: The structure has no interim cash flows. The receiver's position settles once, at the six-month maturity, on the EUR 4.5 million notional, so the identical EUR 300,000 result is reached through a single settlement rather than through a stream of interim payments.

questions.stem: For many investment managers, equity index futures are most likely:

options.A: a speculators' instrument with no portfolio management role.
options.B: a costlier route to index exposure than trading the underlying stocks.
options.C: a low-cost tool for tactical allocation, diversification, and international exposure.

rationales.A: They are an indispensable manager tool, used for tactical allocation shifts, beta adjustment, cash equitization, and rebalancing, so they are not a speculators-only instrument.
rationales.B: Cost runs the other way. Given the liquidity and low transaction costs of the listed futures market, futures are typically the cheapest route to changing index exposure, rather than a more expensive alternative to trading a basket of underlying shares.
rationales.C: Equity index futures are an indispensable tool for many investment managers: they are a low-cost instrument to implement tactical allocation decisions, achieve portfolio diversification, and attain international exposure. They are standardized contracts listed on an exchange, and when the underlying is a stock index, only cash settlement is available at contract expiration. Single stock futures are also available to investors to acquire the desired exposure to a specific stock; that exposure is also achievable with equity forwards, which are over-the-counter contracts used when the counterparties need a customized agreement. The underlying of a single stock futures contract is one specified stock, whose performance the investor can receive or pay, and at expiration the contract could require either cash settlement or physical settlement using the stock.

questions.stem: The number of futures contracts needed to shift a stock portfolio's beta to a target level is most likely:

options.A: the beta gap divided by the futures beta, times the portfolio-to-contract value ratio.
options.B: the three betas multiplied together, times the portfolio-to-contract value ratio.
options.C: the summed betas divided by the futures beta, times the contract-to-portfolio value ratio.

rationales.A: N_f = [(β_T - β_S)/β_f] x (S/F), where β_T is the target beta, β_S is the portfolio beta, β_f is the beta of the futures, S is the market value of the stock portfolio, and F is the value of one futures contract. If the investor wants to increase the portfolio's beta, β_T will exceed β_S, the sign of N_f will be positive, and she must buy futures. If she wants to decrease the beta, β_T will be less than β_S, the sign of N_f will be negative, and she must sell futures. That relationship should make sense: selling futures offsets some of the risk of holding the stock, whereas buying futures adds risk. In the special case in which the goal is to eliminate market risk, β_T is set to zero and the formula reduces to N_f = -(β_S/β_f)(S/F), so the sign of N_f is always negative.
rationales.B: Multiplying the betas together has no meaning here. The hedge ratio is driven by the distance between the current and target beta, N_f = [(β_T - β_S)/β_f] x (S/F), so a portfolio already at its target beta requires no contracts at all.
rationales.C: The numerator is the beta gap, β_T - β_S, not the sum of the two betas, and the value ratio is the portfolio value over the contract value, S/F, not F/S. The correct expression is N_f = [(β_T - β_S)/β_f] x (S/F).

questions.stem: Bianchi wants to move the beta of a GBP 40,000,000 stock portfolio from 0.85 to a target of 1.10 using FTSE 100 futures that have a beta of 1.00 and a value of GBP 73,000 per contract. The appropriate trade is most likely to:

options.A: sell 137 contracts.
options.B: buy 548 contracts.
options.C: buy 137 contracts.

rationales.A: The sign of the hedge ratio sets the direction. N_f = [(1.10 - 0.85)/1.00] x (GBP 40,000,000/GBP 73,000) = +136.99, and a positive N_f means the 137 contracts must be bought. Selling futures would offset part of the risk of holding the stock and drive the effective beta below the current 0.85, away from the 1.10 target.
rationales.B: 548 comes from dividing the full portfolio value by the contract value, GBP 40,000,000/GBP 73,000 = 547.9, while omitting the beta-adjustment factor (β_T - β_S)/β_f = (1.10 - 0.85)/1.00 = 0.25, which scales the count down to 136.99, or 137 contracts.
rationales.C: N_f = [(β_T - β_S)/β_f](S/F) = [(1.10 - 0.85)/1.00] x (GBP 40,000,000/GBP 73,000) = 136.99, rounded to 137 contracts, and the positive sign means the contracts are bought. Verification: if the FTSE 100 rises 2%, the portfolio rises 2% x 0.85 = 1.7%, or GBP 680,000, to GBP 40,680,000, and the profit on the futures is 137 x (GBP 74,460 - GBP 73,000) = GBP 200,020. Adding the futures profit to the value of the stock portfolio gives GBP 40,680,000 + GBP 200,020 = GBP 40,880,020, a return for the combined position of GBP 40,880,020/GBP 40,000,000 - 1 = 0.0220, or 2.2%. Because the market rose 2% and the overall gain was 2.2%, the effective beta was 0.0220/0.020 = 1.10, matching the target beta.

questions.stem: An alternative name for cash equitization is most likely:

options.A: portfolio immunization, or duration matching.
options.B: cash securitization, or cash overlay.
options.C: cash drag, or cash sweep.

rationales.A: Those are fixed-income techniques for managing interest rate risk against a liability or an investment horizon, and are unrelated to equitizing idle cash balances with index futures.
rationales.B: Cash securitization, also known as cash equitization or cash overlay, is a strategy designed to boost returns by finding ways to equitize unintended cash holdings. By purchasing futures contracts, fund managers attempt to replicate the performance of the underlying market in which the cash would have been invested, and the liquidity of the futures market makes doing so relatively easy. An alternative solution is to purchase calls and sell puts on the underlying asset with the same exercise price and expiry date. Because the holding is cash, its beta is zero, so β_S = 0 and the number of futures with beta β_f to be purchased in a cash equitization transaction is N_f = (β_T/β_f)(S/F).
rationales.C: Cash drag is the performance shortfall that cash equitization is meant to cure, not another name for the strategy, and a cash sweep is a treasury mechanism for moving idle balances. The strategy itself is called cash securitization or cash overlay.

questions.stem: Fujiwara wants to equitize JPY 140,000,000 of excess cash that has built up in a yen-denominated fund indexed to the Nikkei 225, using index futures quoted at 23,000 with a contract multiplier of JPY 1,000 per index point and a beta of 1.00. The number of futures contracts she should buy is closest to:

rationales.A: 6,087 divides the cash balance by the quoted futures price, JPY 140,000,000/JPY 23,000, instead of by the full value of one contract, F = 23,000 x JPY 1,000 = JPY 23,000,000. Applying the multiplier gives 6.087, or six contracts.
rationales.B: A cash holding has no equity exposure, so β_S = 0 and the hedge ratio reduces to N_f = (β_T/β_f)(S/F) = (1.00/1.00)(JPY 140,000,000/JPY 23,000,000) = 6.087, rounded to 6. The contract value of JPY 23,000,000 follows from the quoted price of 23,000 index points multiplied by the JPY 1,000 per index point contract multiplier. The appropriate number of futures to buy to equitize the portfolio's excess cash position, based on the data provided, is therefore six contracts, which replicates the return on the fund's target index on the idle cash.
rationales.C: 61 treats each contract as worth JPY 2,300,000. With a quoted price of 23,000 and a multiplier of JPY 1,000 per index point, each contract is worth JPY 23,000,000, so N_f = JPY 140,000,000/JPY 23,000,000 = 6.087, or six contracts.

questions.stem: A portfolio manager wants to hedge 30% of a USD 100,000,000 equity portfolio that carries average market risk, using one-month S&P 500 futures quoted at 2,700 with a contract multiplier of USD 250. The actual futures contract price is closest to:

rationales.A: The quoted index level is multiplied by the contract multiplier, not divided by it. The actual futures price is 2,700 x $250 = $675,000.
rationales.B: $270,000 applies a $100 multiplier. The S&P 500 futures contract multiplier is $250, so the actual futures price is 2,700 x $250 = $675,000.
rationales.C: Given the multiplier of $250, the actual futures price equals $675,000 (= 2,700 x $250). Assuming the portfolio to be hedged carries average market risk, meaning a beta of 1.0, to hedge 30% of the $100 million portfolio the manager would want to sell 44 S&P 500 futures contracts, determined as $30,000,000/(2,700 x $250) = 44.444, rounded to 44 contracts. If the portfolio instead carried above-market risk, say with a beta of 1.10, the number of contracts needed to hedge would increase by that factor.

questions.stem: For the portion of an equity portfolio allocation that it covers, a total return swap is most likely to:

options.A: leave the equity risk in place and add a funding cost.
options.B: convert the allocation into additional equity exposure at a higher beta.
options.C: convert the allocation into money market equivalent returns.

rationales.A: The swap removes the equity risk of the portion it covers, which is the whole point of the transfer, rather than leaving that risk in place. What the holder gives up is the equity return on that portion, received back as a money market equivalent return.
rationales.B: The conversion runs from equity toward a money market return, not from equity toward leveraged equity. The swap pays away the total performance of the covered portion and receives a money market equivalent return in exchange, so exposure and beta fall rather than rise.
rationales.C: A total return swap effectively removes the risk associated with the portion of the equity portfolio allocation it covers and converts it into money market equivalent returns. As a test of reasonableness, a portfolio comprising 70% equities and 30% money market instruments assumed to earn 2%, or 1% over six months, would achieve a return of 3.8% (= 0.7 x 5% + 0.3 x [2%/2]), or $3.8 million on $100 million, in a bullish scenario in which equities return 5%. In a bearish scenario in which equities return -5%, the return would be -3.2% (= 0.7 x -5% + 0.3 x [2%/2]), or -$3.2 million on the initial $100 million portfolio. Swapping away 30% of the equity allocation therefore leaves 70% equity exposure plus a money market return on the remaining 30%.

questions.stem: A £40 million portfolio with an original beta of 0.85 uses a futures overlay targeting a beta of 1.10. Over the period, the market rises 2% and the combined position gains 2.2%. The effective beta achieved is most likely:

rationales.A: Effective beta on the combined position equals the realized return on that position divided by the market return. The market rose 2% and the overlay-adjusted portfolio gained 2.2%, so the effective beta is 0.0220/0.0200 = 1.10, exactly the target beta. That match is the check on the overlay: the number of contracts came from N_f = [(β_T − β_S)/β_f](S/F), and because the combined return scaled up by 1.10 rather than 0.85, the £40 million of equity plus the long futures position behaved as if it were a single portfolio with a beta of 1.10. The hedge ratio formula therefore worked correctly in achieving the intended market exposure.
rationales.B: An effective beta of 1.00 would mean the combined position merely tracked the market, earning the same 2% the index earned. The position gained 2.2%, which is 1.10 times the 2% market move, so the realized beta is above 1.00. An index-matching beta of 1.00 was also never the objective here: the futures were bought to lift exposure from the original 0.85 to the 1.10 target, not to neutralize the portfolio's tilt relative to the market.
rationales.C: 0.85 is the original beta of the £40 million equity portfolio, measured before the futures overlay was put in place. Buying futures raised market exposure from that starting point to the 1.10 target, and the outcome confirms it: a 2.2% gain against a 2% market move gives 0.0220/0.0200 = 1.10. The effective beta would have stayed at 0.85 only if no futures had been traded at all, in which case the 2% market move would have produced a gain of roughly 1.7%.

questions.stem: For an investor using equity index futures to adjust a portfolio's beta, the required futures trade is most likely:

options.A: no futures trade, with target beta set equal to portfolio beta, to eliminate market risk.
options.B: a sale of futures, to increase portfolio beta.
options.C: a purchase of futures, to increase portfolio beta.

rationales.A: Eliminating market risk means setting the target beta to zero, not setting it equal to the portfolio's own beta. With β_T = 0 the hedge ratio N_f = [(β_T − β_S)/β_f](S/F) reduces to N_f = −(β_S/β_f)(S/F), and the sign of that expression is always negative, so the full hedge is implemented by selling futures rather than by trading none. Setting β_T equal to β_S does make the numerator zero and so calls for no contracts, but that is the case of leaving market exposure exactly as it is, which is the opposite of hedging it away.
rationales.B: Selling futures offsets part of the risk of holding the stock, so a sale lowers beta rather than raising it. When the investor wants more market exposure, β_T exceeds β_S, the numerator (β_T − β_S) in N_f = [(β_T − β_S)/β_f](S/F) is positive, and the sign of N_f is positive, which means contracts must be bought. A negative N_f, and therefore a sale, arises only when the target beta lies below the current portfolio beta, with the fully hedged case β_T = 0 as the extreme.
rationales.C: If the investor wants to increase the portfolio's beta, β_T will exceed β_S and the sign of N_f = [(β_T − β_S)/β_f](S/F) will be positive, which means she must buy futures. If she wants to decrease the beta, β_T will be less than β_S, the sign of N_f will be negative, and she must sell futures. This relationship should make sense: selling futures offsets some of the risk of holding the stock, whereas buying futures adds risk. In the special case in which the goal is to eliminate market risk, β_T is set to zero and the formula reduces to N_f = −(β_S/β_f)(S/F); the sign of N_f is then always negative, which again makes sense, because hedging away all the market risk requires futures to be sold.
