questions.stem: For an investor holding a long equity portfolio, the effect of adding long volatility exposure is best described as:

options.A: unrelated to the portfolio's performance.
options.B: an effective hedge, especially during extreme market moves.
options.C: an amplifier of losses, because volatility falls as prices fall.

rationales.A: The link between volatility and equity returns is neither absent nor incidental. Empirical studies identify a negative correlation between volatility and stock index returns, and that correlation becomes pronounced during stock market downturns — that is, it is strongest precisely when the equity holder most needs protection. Because the relationship is both reliable and asymmetric in the investor's favor, volatility futures and variance swaps are used deliberately as equity hedges, and many investors now treat volatility as an asset class in its own right.
rationales.B: Long volatility exposure can be an effective hedge against a sell-off in a long equity portfolio, notably during periods of extreme market movements. Empirical studies have identified a negative correlation between volatility and stock index returns that becomes pronounced during stock market downturns, so the hedge pays most when the equity book is losing most. With the introduction of volatility futures and variance swaps, many investors now consider volatility an asset class in itself. Variance swaps in particular have a valuable convexity feature — as realized volatility increases (decreases), the positive (negative) swap payoffs increase (decrease) — which makes them especially attractive for hedging long equity portfolios, because the payoff accelerates in the tail rather than growing in a straight line.
rationales.C: Volatility rises in a sell-off; it does not fall. The negative correlation between index returns and volatility is exactly what makes a long volatility position a hedge: as prices drop, volatility increases and the long volatility position gains, offsetting part of the equity loss rather than compounding it. The effect strengthens in extreme downturns, and with a variance swap the convexity of the payoff means the gain grows faster than the move in volatility itself.

questions.stem: The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) is most likely a measure of:

options.A: expected S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days.
options.B: realized S&P 500 volatility over the past 30 days.
options.C: expected S&P 500 dividend yields over the next year.

rationales.A: The CBOE Volatility Index, known as the VIX or the "fear index," is a measure of investors' expectations of volatility in the S&P 500 over the next 30 days. It is calculated and published by the Chicago Board Options Exchange and is based on the prices of S&P 500 Index options, so it is an implied, forward-looking number rather than a statistic computed from past returns. The CBOE began publishing real-time VIX data in 1993, and in 2004 VIX futures were introduced. Investors cannot invest directly in the VIX; they must use VIX futures contracts, which offer a pure play on the level of expected stock market volatility regardless of the direction of the S&P 500.
rationales.B: The VIX is forward looking. It is backed out of the prices of S&P 500 Index options, so it reports implied volatility over the coming 30 days, not volatility realized over the 30 days just ended. Realized volatility is computed from the historical return series; the two can diverge sharply, and the gap between them is itself the subject of variance swap trades.
rationales.C: Dividends are not the index's subject at all. The VIX gauges expected S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days — hence its nickname, the "fear index" — and it is derived from S&P 500 Index option prices, which carry information about the expected magnitude of index moves rather than about the cash the index constituents will pay out.

questions.stem: Volatility indexes for European equity markets are most likely:

options.A: available, and reflect expectations of near- to long-term volatility.
options.B: available, but measure realized historical volatility.
options.C: unavailable.

rationales.A: A family of volatility indexes has been introduced for European equity markets, and they are designed to reflect market expectations of near-term to long-term volatility. The most well known of these is the VSTOXX index, which is based on real-time option prices on the EURO STOXX 50 index. The family also includes the VDAX-NEW Index, based on DAX stock index options. Like the VIX in the United States, these indexes read expectations out of current option prices, so they span a range of horizons rather than reporting a single backward-looking statistic.
rationales.B: These indexes are implied-volatility gauges, built the same way the VIX is. VSTOXX is computed from real-time option prices on the EURO STOXX 50 and VDAX-NEW from DAX stock index options, so each reflects market expectations of volatility from the near term out to the long term, not volatility already realized in the historical return series.
rationales.C: A European family does exist. VSTOXX, based on real-time option prices on the EURO STOXX 50 index, is the best known, and VDAX-NEW, based on DAX stock index options, belongs to the same family. They are designed to reflect market expectations of near-term to long-term volatility in European equity markets.

questions.stem: When volatility is expected to remain stable over the near to long term, the term structure of VIX futures is most likely:

options.A: flat.
options.B: in contango, whatever the volatility expectations.
options.C: in backwardation.

rationales.A: An expectation that volatility will hold steady from the near term out to the long term produces a flat term structure of VIX futures: there is no reason for contracts of different maturities to be priced apart. The shape of the VIX futures curve is always changing, and the other two shapes carry their own messages. Backwardation typically signals that investors expect more volatility in the short term and therefore require higher prices for shorter-term contracts than for longer-term ones. Contango is an upward-sloped curve, and higher longer-term VIX futures prices are interpreted as an expectation that the VIX will rise because of increasing long-term volatility; such a curve can be steep for VIX buyers, with several volatility points between consecutive expiries. The shape at any moment reflects the current volatility environment, investors' expectations, and buying and selling activity, and it can move from positively sloped to flat or inverted within a few months.
rationales.B: The VIX futures curve is not always upward sloping. It can be flat, in backwardation, or in contango, depending on the volatility environment and investors' expectations, and the shape can change from positively sloped to flat or inverted within a few months as that environment shifts. Contango specifically conveys an expectation that the VIX will rise because of increasing long-term volatility, which is a particular view rather than a permanent feature of the market.
rationales.C: Backwardation is the shape produced by an expectation of more volatility in the short term than in the long term: investors then require higher prices for shorter-term contracts than for longer-term ones, so the curve slopes downward. An expectation that volatility will remain stable over the near to long term prices all maturities alike and therefore produces a flat term structure instead.

questions.stem: The behaviour of VIX futures prices as expiration approaches is most likely:

options.A: divergence from spot VIX, widening the basis at settlement.
options.B: roll-down profits on a long back-month position when the curve is in contango.
options.C: convergence to spot VIX, with the two equal at expiration.

rationales.A: VIX futures converge to the spot VIX as expiration approaches, so the basis collapses toward zero rather than widening; at expiration the futures price and the spot index must be equal. That convergence is why traders can calculate a daily roll at all: the daily roll is the difference between the front-month VIX futures price and the VIX spot price, divided by the number of business days until the contract settles. A basis that widened into settlement would leave an arbitrage open at expiry.
rationales.B: In contango the futures price sits above spot, so as expiration approaches and volatility expectations are unchanged, the futures price is pulled down toward the spot VIX. Assuming the basis declines linearly until settlement, a trader who is long back-month VIX futures therefore realizes roll-down losses, not profits. Roll-down profits accrue to the long position in the opposite case, when the term structure is in backwardation and the futures price is pulled up toward spot.
rationales.C: VIX futures converge to the spot VIX as expiration approaches, so the two must be equal at expiration. When the VIX futures curve is in contango (backwardation), and assuming volatility expectations remain unchanged, the VIX futures price will get "pulled" closer to the VIX spot price, decreasing (increasing) in price as it approaches expiration. Traders calculate the daily roll as the difference between the front-month VIX futures price and the VIX spot price, divided by the number of business days until the VIX futures contract settles. Assuming that the basis declines linearly until settlement, when the term structure is in contango (backwardation) the trader who is long in back-month VIX futures would realize roll-down losses (profits).

questions.stem: The volatility exposure provided by exchange-listed VIX options is most likely:

options.A: symmetric and linear, identical to a VIX futures position.
options.B: nonexistent, because no VIX options have been introduced.
options.C: asymmetrical with respect to increases or decreases in anticipated volatility.

rationales.A: Asymmetry is the defining feature of VIX options and the reason they were introduced alongside the already-trading futures. A futures position gains and loses in a straight line with the VIX; an option position does not. A call buyer participates in a rise in anticipated volatility while risking only the premium, and a put buyer profits from a decline on the same terms, so the exposure is one-sided rather than symmetric and linear.
rationales.B: VIX options were introduced in 2006 and trade actively. They are European style, and their prices depend on the prices of VIX futures with similar expirations, because market makers in VIX options typically hedge the risk of their option positions using VIX futures. Volatility is therefore tradable in listed form through both futures and options, even though investors cannot invest in the spot VIX directly.
rationales.C: In 2006, VIX options were introduced, providing an asymmetrical exposure to potential increases or decreases in anticipated volatility. VIX options are European style, and their prices depend on the prices of VIX futures with similar expirations, because the market makers of VIX options typically hedge the risk of their option positions using VIX futures. To understand the use of VIX calls and puts, it is important to recognize that increases in the VIX, and in VIX futures, are negatively correlated with the prices of equity assets. A trader or investor would purchase VIX call options when expecting volatility to increase owing to a significant sell-off in the equity market. VIX put options, in contrast, would be bought to profit from an expectation that volatility will decrease because of stable equity market conditions.

questions.stem: A variance swap is best described as:

options.A: an instrument for directional bets on implied versus realized volatility.
options.B: an instrument whose payoff is linear in realized volatility.
options.C: an exchange-traded option on the VIX index.

rationales.A: Variance swaps are instruments used by investors for taking directional bets on implied versus realized volatility, for speculative or hedging purposes. The term "variance swap" refers to the fact that these instruments have a payoff analogous to that of a swap: the buyer of the contract will pay the difference between the fixed variance strike agreed on in the contract and the realized variance, annualized, on the underlying over the period specified, applied to a variance notional. There is no exchange of cash at the contract's inception or during the life of the swap. The payoff at expiration of a long variance position will be positive when realized variance is greater than the swap's variance strike and negative when realized variance is less than the strike.
rationales.B: The payoff is linear in variance, that is, in volatility squared, and therefore convex in volatility itself. That convexity is a large part of the instrument's appeal: as realized volatility increases or decreases, the positive or negative swap payoffs increase or decrease more than proportionately, which is what makes variance swaps attractive for hedging a long equity portfolio. A contract linear in realized volatility would be a volatility swap, a different instrument with no such convexity.
rationales.C: A variance swap is an over-the-counter contract, not a listed option on the VIX. The buyer pays the difference between a fixed variance strike and realized annualized variance on the underlying, applied to a variance notional, with no cash exchanged at inception or during the life of the swap. Listed VIX options, by contrast, are European-style exchange-traded contracts whose prices depend on VIX futures of similar expiration.

questions.stem: The settlement amount on a variance swap at expiration is most likely:

options.A: the variance notional times realized volatility less the volatility strike.
options.B: the vega notional times realized variance less the variance strike.
options.C: the variance notional times realized variance less the variance strike.

rationales.A: Settlement is computed in variance terms, in squared units, not in volatility levels: the bracketed difference is realized variance minus the variance strike, where realized variance = 252 × [Σ R_i²/(N − 1)] with R_i = ln(P_i+1/P_i) and N the number of days observed. Subtracting a volatility strike from a realized volatility would describe a volatility swap, whose payoff is linear in volatility and so lacks the convexity that the variance contract provides.
rationales.B: The multiplier is the variance notional, not the vega notional. Vega notional is the market's quoting convention, because it expresses the contract's exposure per volatility point and is more intuitive to trade on, but it must first be converted into a variance notional before it can be applied to the difference between realized variance and the variance strike. Applying a vega notional directly to a difference stated in variance units mixes the two conventions and overstates or understates the payment.
rationales.C: Settlement amount at time T = (variance notional) × (realized variance − variance strike). If the payment amount is positive, the swap seller pays the swap buyer; if it is negative, the swap buyer pays the swap seller. Realized variance is calculated as 252 × [Σ R_i²/(N − 1)], where R_i = ln(P_i+1/P_i) and N is the number of days observed. Both terms inside the parentheses are therefore in squared, annualized units, and the variance notional converts that squared difference into a cash amount; a vega notional quote has to be converted to a variance notional before it can be used here.

questions.stem: By market convention, the trade size of a variance swap is most likely agreed in:

options.A: variance notional only.
options.B: vega notional or variance notional, which are identical.
options.C: vega notional.

rationales.A: Market convention quotes the vega notional, the approximate profit and loss per volatility point, and converts to variance notional only for settlement: variance notional = vega notional / (2 × strike). Sizing the trade in variance notional is not how the market talks about it; the variance notional is the derived quantity used to calculate the exact payoff.
rationales.B: The two differ by construction: variance notional = vega notional / (2 × strike). A $50,000 vega notional struck at a volatility of 20 corresponds to a variance notional of $50,000/(2 × 20) = 1,250. They also measure different things: the vega notional is the average profit and loss for a 1% change in volatility from the strike, while the variance notional is the multiplier applied to the difference between realized variance and the variance strike.
rationales.C: Variance swap traders typically agree on two things: the trade size, expressed in vega notional, N_Vega, rather than in variance notional, and the strike, X, which represents the expected future variance of the underlying but is quoted as a volatility rather than a variance. Quoting the size in vega notional is intuitive because the vega notional represents the average profit and loss of the swap for a 1% change in volatility from the strike; with a vega notional of $50,000, the profit and loss for one volatility point of difference between realized volatility and the strike will be close to $50,000. That is an approximation, because the variance swap payoff is convex and the profit and loss is not linear in changes in realized volatility. To calculate the exact payoff, the variance strike is the strike squared and the variance notional is defined as Variance notional = Vega notional / (2 × Strike price).

questions.stem: A variance swap is written with a vega notional of $50,000 and a volatility strike of 20. The variance notional is closest to:

rationales.A: Variance notional = vega notional / (2 × strike) = $50,000/(2 × 20) = 1,250. That 1,250 is the multiplier applied to the difference between realized variance and the variance strike, so it drives both settlement at expiration and any mark-to-market before it. Taking the valuation six months into a one-year swap, with realized volatility of 16% over the elapsed period, a fair strike of 19% on the remaining period and a 2.5% discount rate: the variance strike on the existing swap is 20² = 400, realized volatility squared is 16² = 256, implied volatility squared is 19² = 361, and the present value factor is 1/[1 + (2.5% × 6/12)] = 0.987654. The swap value is then 1,250 × 0.987654 × [(6/12) × 256 + (6/12) × 361 − 400] = −$112,962.93, so a seller of the swap carries a positive mark-to-market of $112,963.
rationales.B: This divides the vega notional by the strike alone. The vega notional is divided by twice the strike: variance notional = vega notional / (2 × strike) = $50,000/(2 × 20) = 1,250, not 2,500. Using 2,500 would double every settlement and mark-to-market amount the swap produces.
rationales.C: This multiplies by (2 × strike) instead of dividing by it. Variance notional = vega notional / (2 × strike) = $50,000/(2 × 20) = 1,250; 2,000,000 overstates it by a factor of (2 × 20)² = 1,600, since the operation is inverted rather than merely mis-scaled.

questions.stem: Santos is short a one-year variance swap with a volatility strike of 20 and a variance notional of 1,250. Realized volatility over the year is 18%. Settlement at expiration most likely results in Santos:

options.A: receiving $2,500.
options.B: receiving $95,000.
options.C: paying $95,000.

rationales.A: Settlement runs on variance units, not on the difference in volatility levels. Settlement = variance notional × (realized variance − variance strike) = 1,250 × (18² − 20²) = 1,250 × (324 − 400) = −$95,000. Applying the volatility difference instead, 1,250 × (18 − 20) = −$2,500, gets the direction right but understates the amount by a wide margin, because the squares of realized volatility and the strike enter the payoff rather than their levels.
rationales.B: Settlement = variance notional × (realized variance − variance strike) = 1,250 × (18² − 20²) = 1,250 × (324 − 400) = −$95,000. When the settlement amount is positive the swap seller pays the swap buyer, and when it is negative the swap buyer pays the swap seller. The amount here is negative and Santos is the seller, so Santos receives $95,000 from the swap buyer: realized volatility of 18% came in below the 20 strike, which is the outcome the short position is positioned for.
rationales.C: Santos is short the variance swap, that is, the seller. The settlement amount, 1,250 × (18² − 20²) = 1,250 × (324 − 400) = −$95,000, is negative, and a negative settlement means the swap buyer pays the swap seller. Santos therefore receives $95,000 rather than paying it; realized volatility finishing below the strike is precisely what makes the seller's position profitable, so the direction of the cash flow is reversed here.

questions.stem: The payoff of a variance swap with respect to volatility is best described as:

options.A: convex.
options.B: linear.
options.C: concave.

rationales.A: The payoff of a variance swap is convex in volatility. The convexity arises because being long a variance swap is equivalent to being long a basket of options and short the underlying asset, typically by selling a futures contract; the long position is therefore long gamma and its payoff curves upward. This characteristic allows volatility sellers to sell variance swaps at a higher price than at-the-money options, because the convex payoff profile is attractive to investors who want a long volatility position as a tail risk hedge.
rationales.B: A linear payoff would describe a futures-like exposure to volatility. The variance swap settles on realized variance, the square of volatility, so in volatility terms the payoff curves rather than running straight: it is convex and long gamma, which is why the swap can be sold at a higher price than an at-the-money option on the same underlying.
rationales.C: The payoff is convex rather than concave, so gains accelerate as realized volatility rises instead of flattening out. The long position replicates a basket of options against a short in the underlying and is long gamma; the absence of a cap on the upside is exactly what makes a long variance swap attractive as a tail risk hedge, and what lets the seller charge more than for an at-the-money option.

questions.stem: As a variance swap approaches expiration, its sensitivity to changes in implied volatility most likely:

options.A: remains constant.
options.B: diminishes.
options.C: increases.

rationales.A: The sensitivity is not constant. Only the period from the valuation date to maturity, T − t, is still valued off implied volatility; variance over the elapsed period is already locked in as realized variance. As T − t shrinks, a given change in implied volatility applies to an ever-smaller share of the swap's total variance, so its effect on value falls steadily rather than holding steady.
rationales.B: The sensitivity of a variance swap to changes in implied volatility diminishes over time. As the swap approaches expiration, changes in implied volatility have less effect on the swap's value because the remaining time period, T − t, decreases, and only that remaining period is marked off implied volatility. The variance already realized over the elapsed period is fixed, so the implied-volatility term carries progressively less weight in the valuation.
rationales.C: The opposite holds. Implied volatility prices only the remaining period, T − t, which shrinks toward zero as expiration approaches, so the variance swap's sensitivity to changes in implied volatility diminishes rather than increases. What grows over the swap's life is the weight of realized variance, which is already determined and no longer sensitive to the implied level.

drills.los_text: demonstrate the use of derivatives to achieve targeted equity and interest rate risk exposures

questions.stem: A client holds 100,000 shares of Tundra Corporation, trading at €14, acquired many years ago on a very low tax basis, and does not want to sell them; no exchange-traded options on the stock are available. The most appropriate way to safeguard the value of the position is to:

options.A: enter an equity swap exchanging Tundra's total return for a floating reference rate.
options.B: sell the shares outright.
options.C: buy exchange-traded put options on the shares.

rationales.A: At €14 per share on 100,000 shares the position is worth €1.4 million. An equity swap can exchange the total return on the shares, which includes both price performance and the dividends received, for the reference rate return on that same €1.4 million. That transfers the price risk without selling the stock, so the very low tax basis is left undisturbed and no gain is realized. The remaining design choice is the horizon: the manager must determine the period over which protection is needed and match the swap tenor to it, for example a six-month tenor against a reference rate of 0.34% annually.
rationales.B: Transaction costs are not the only consideration. The shares have been held for many years on a very low tax basis, so an outright sale realizes a large taxable gain, and the client does not want to sell in any case. The total return swap sheds the €1.4 million of price exposure while leaving both the shares and the tax basis in place, which is why it is preferred over liquidation here.
rationales.C: Exchange-traded options are unavailable on this stock, and that gap is precisely what sends the hedge into the over-the-counter market. Listed options cannot be the complete solution when they do not trade on the name; an over-the-counter equity swap on the single name supplies the exposure transfer instead, with the tenor set to the period of protection required.

questions.stem: A client's equity swap exchanges the total return on 100,000 Tundra shares, priced at €14, for a 0.34% annual reference rate on the €1.4 million position. Over the first six months Tundra pays a €0.10 dividend and its share price rises 1%. The outcome of that period is most likely:

options.A: a 1.71% stock return, with the client paying.
options.B: a 1.71% stock return, with the client receiving.
options.C: a 1.00% stock return, with the client paying.

rationales.A: The total return on the stock includes the dividend as well as the price move: [(14 × 1.01) − 14 + 0.10]/14 = 1.71%. For a six-month period the reference rate return is half the annual rate, or 0.17%. Tundra's total return exceeds the six-month reference rate return, so the net amount is (1.71% − 0.17%) × €1.4 million = €21,620, a positive figure. The client pays away the stock's total return under the swap, so the client pays €21,620 to the swap counterparty.
rationales.B: The amount is right and the direction is reversed. (1.71% − 0.17%) × €1.4 million = +€21,620, which means the stock's total return outran the reference rate return. Under this swap the client pays the stock's total return and receives the reference rate, so a positive figure is paid to the counterparty rather than received from it. The client collects only in the opposite case, when the stock's total return falls short of the reference rate.
rationales.C: This counts only the 1% price move and drops the €0.10 dividend. A total return swap passes through dividends as well as price performance, so the six-month total return on the stock is [(14 × 1.01) − 14 + 0.10]/14 = 1.71%, not 1.00%. The direction of the flow is right, since even 1.00% exceeds the 0.17% six-month reference rate return and the client pays, but the amount owed is (1.71% − 0.17%) × €1.4 million = €21,620, larger than a 1.00% return would imply.

questions.stem: A client's equity swap exchanges the total return on 100,000 Tundra shares, priced at €14, for a 0.34% annual reference rate on the €1.4 million position. Over the six months Tundra pays a €0.10 dividend and its share price falls 1%. The outcome of that period is most likely:

options.A: a −0.29% stock return, with the client paying.
options.B: a −1.00% stock return, with the client receiving.
options.C: a −0.29% stock return, with the client receiving.

rationales.A: The return is right and the direction of the cash flow is reversed. With the dividend included, the stock's total return is [(14 × 0.99) − 14 + 0.10]/14 = −0.29%, below the six-month reference rate return of 0.17%, so the net amount is (−0.29% − 0.17%) × €1.4 million = −€6,380. Because the figure is negative, the client receives the negative stock return and the reference rate return from the swap counterparty, a positive cash inflow of €6,380, instead of paying it out.
rationales.B: This drops the €0.10 dividend. The dividend partially offsets the 1% price decline, so the total return on the stock is [(14 × 0.99) − 14 + 0.10]/14 = −0.29%, not −1.00%. The client does receive on this settlement, but the amount follows from the correct return: (−0.29% − 0.17%) × €1.4 million = −€6,380, an inflow of €6,380 rather than the larger sum a −1.00% return would produce.
rationales.C: The total return on the stock is [(14 × 0.99) − 14 + 0.10]/14 = −0.29%, since the €0.10 dividend offsets part of the 1% price fall. Tundra's total return is less than the six-month reference rate return of 0.17%, so the net amount is (−0.29% − 0.17%) × €1.4 million = −€6,380, a negative figure. The client therefore receives the negative stock return plus the reference rate return from the swap counterparty, which is a positive cash inflow of €6,380.

questions.stem: McMillian wants to equitize £20 million of cash against the FTSE 100, where one index futures contract is priced at £79,000 and both the target beta and the futures beta are 1.0. She should most likely:

options.A: buy 253 contracts.
options.B: sell 253 contracts.
options.C: buy 25 contracts.

rationales.A: The contract count for a synthetic index strategy is N_f = (β_T/β_f)(S/F) = (1.0/1.0)(20,000,000/79,000) = 253.16, rounded to 253. Buying 253 FTSE 100 futures gains index exposure on the notional amount of £20 million. Both the target beta, β_T, and the beta of the futures contract, β_f, equal 1.0, so the ratio is one and the overlay simply replicates FTSE 100 performance on the cash reserve, which minimizes tracking error against a fully invested portfolio.
rationales.B: The contract count is right and the sign is wrong. Equitizing idle cash means adding long index exposure, so the 253 contracts must be bought. Selling 253 contracts would set a short index position against the cash, leaving the £20 million with no equity exposure at all and introducing a new short exposure instead of replicating the FTSE 100 return.
rationales.C: Decimal slip: £20,000,000/£79,000 = 253.16, so 253 contracts are required, not 25. Each contract carries £79,000 of index exposure, so 25 contracts would equitize just under £2 million, roughly a tenth of the cash position, and most of the cash drag would remain.

questions.stem: McMillian holds £230 million of UK stocks plus £20 million of cash equitized by buying 253 FTSE 100 Index futures contracts at £7,900, each index point worth £10, with the cash invested at a 0.63% annual floating rate. Three months later the FTSE 100 has risen 5%. The result for the £250 million portfolio is most likely:

options.A: a futures gain and a 5% combined return.
options.B: a futures loss and a return below 5%.
options.C: a futures gain and a 4.6% combined return.

rationales.A: With the index up 5%, the original £230 million invested in UK stocks increases to £241.5 million and the price of the FTSE 100 Index futures contract rises from £7,900 to £8,282.5. Interest on the cash invested at the three-month floating rate amounts to £20,000,000 × 0.63% × 90/360 = £31,500. The futures were bought at £7,900 and settle at £8,282.5, a gain of 382.5 index points, each point worth £10, on 253 contracts, for a total cash inflow of 382.5 × £10 × 253 = £967,725. Adding the futures profit and the cash reserves plus interest gives a total portfolio value of £241,500,000 + £20,000,000 + £967,725 + £31,500 = £262,499,225, and the rate of return on the combined position is £262,499,225/£250,000,000 − 1 = 0.05, or 5%. Without the strategy the return would have been slightly over 4.6%.
rationales.B: The futures position gained rather than lost. McMillian bought the contracts and the index rose, so the long futures earned 382.5 index points × £10 per point × 253 contracts = £967,725, which adds to the stock gain instead of offsetting it. A loss on the overlay would require a short futures position; as structured, the futures profit plus £31,500 of interest lifts the combined return to exactly the index's 5% rather than holding it below.
rationales.C: Slightly over 4.6% is the return the portfolio would have earned without the overlay, held back by £20 million of idle cash. With the overlay in place, the futures gain of £967,725 and interest of £31,500 bring total portfolio value to £241,500,000 + £20,000,000 + £967,725 + £31,500 = £262,499,225, a return of £262,499,225/£250,000,000 − 1 = 5%. The strategy closes the cash drag, so the combined position matches the index instead of lagging it.

questions.stem: Rossi manages a €500 million portfolio allocated 70% to stocks and 30% to government bonds. Bearish on eurozone stocks other than German shares and bullish on Italian bonds over a three-month horizon, he wants to cut the equity allocation to 60%, held at equal weights in Italian and German shares, and raise government bonds to 40%. Regarding this portfolio and its rebalancing, the most accurate statement is that:

options.A: the portfolio starts as German equities and French government bonds.
options.B: the rebalancing requires selling the underlying shares and bonds in the cash market.
options.C: the portfolio starts as Italian equities and Italian government bonds.

rationales.A: Before the rebalancing, the book is 70% Italian stocks, with a beta of 1.1 with respect to the FTSE MIB Index, and 30% Italian government bonds (BTPs) with a modified duration of 6.45. German shares are a target exposure Rossi does not yet hold — they arrive only as part of the new 60% equity allocation, at a weight of 30%, with a beta of 0.9 with respect to the DAX Index — and French government bonds play no part in the portfolio at all, before or after.
rationales.B: The overlay is what accomplishes the shift, which is why the cash positions are left alone. Rossi sells FTSE MIB futures to shed Italian equity exposure, buys DAX futures to add German equity exposure, and buys BTP futures to add Italian bond exposure, so no Italian shares and no BTPs change hands. Keeping the physical holdings preserves their tax basis and the voting rights that go with them, avoids the transaction costs of trading a large book, and lets a three-month view be expressed and then reversed quickly.
rationales.C: The €500 million portfolio starts at 70% stocks, all Italian, with a beta of 1.1 with respect to the FTSE MIB Index, and 30% Italian government bonds (BTPs), whose modified duration is 6.45. Rossi wants the overall equity allocation down 10 percentage points to 60%, with the same 30% weight in Italian shares (€150 million) and German shares (€150 million, beta 0.9 with respect to the DAX Index), and the allocation to BTPs up 10 percentage points to 40% (€200 million). In summary, he needs to remove €100 million of exposure to Italian stocks, add €50 million of exposure to German stocks, and add €50 million of exposure to Italian bonds, which he can do with futures on the FTSE MIB, the DAX and BTPs rather than by trading the securities themselves.

questions.stem: Grant manages a portfolio with a target allocation of 40% stocks and 60% bonds. Over the last month its value has risen from €100 million to €106 million, and it now holds €46 million of European stocks, with a beta of 1.2, and €60 million of German bunds. She will rebalance with EURO STOXX 50 index futures, which have a contract value of €35,000 and a beta of 1.0. To return the equity allocation to target, Grant is most likely to:

options.A: reduce equity exposure by €3.6 million.
options.B: increase equity exposure by €3.6 million.
options.C: reduce equity exposure by €6.0 million.

rationales.A: The 40% equity target applies to what the portfolio is worth now: 0.40 × €106,000,000 = €42,400,000, against €46,000,000 of European stocks actually held, which is 43.4% of the portfolio. Equity exposure therefore has to come down by €3,604,000, or 0.034 × €106,000,000, and Grant sells EURO STOXX 50 futures to do it. The market value involved in the transaction is S = €3,604,000, the stocks' beta is βS = 1.2 and the target beta on that slice is βT = 0, while the futures have a contract value F of €35,000 and a beta βf of 1.0, so Nf = [(βT − βS)/βf] × (S/F) = [(0.0 − 1.2)/1.0] × (€3,604,000/€35,000) = −123.57. The negative sign is the sale: Grant sells 124 contracts after rounding.
rationales.B: The direction runs the other way. The stocks have drifted above target rather than below it — €46,000,000 held against a target of 0.40 × €106,000,000 = €42,400,000, which is 43.4% against 40% — so the €3,604,000 adjustment is a reduction, achieved by selling EURO STOXX 50 futures. Buying futures would add equity beta and push the allocation further above the 40% target.
rationales.C: €6.0 million is the gap measured against the portfolio's old value. The target weight applies to the current €106,000,000, so the equity target is 0.40 × €106,000,000 = €42,400,000, not 0.40 × €100,000,000 = €40,000,000. The reduction needed is €46,000,000 − €42,400,000 = €3,604,000, equivalently 0.034 × €106,000,000, rather than €6,000,000.

questions.stem: Grant already holds €60 million of German bunds and wants to add €3,604,000 of bund exposure at a target modified duration of 9.5, using Euro-Bund futures whose cheapest-to-deliver bond has a basis point value of €84.63 and a conversion factor of 0.619489. Her futures trade is closest to:

options.A: 25 contracts bought.
options.B: 25 contracts sold.
options.C: 417 contracts bought.

rationales.A: The target basis point value is computed on the exposure being added, not on the bonds already owned: BPVT = MDURT × 0.01% × MVP = 9.5 × 0.0001 × €3,604,000 = €3,424. There is no existing futures position, so BPVP is zero and the hedge is BPVHR = [(BPVT − BPVP)/BPVCTD] × CF = [(€3,424 − 0)/€84.63] × 0.619489 = 25.06, about 25 contracts. The hedge ratio is positive because duration exposure is being added, so Grant buys 25 Euro-Bund futures contracts.
rationales.B: Selling would strip duration out of the portfolio, which is the opposite of what Grant wants. She is adding €3,604,000 of bund exposure at a target modified duration of 9.5, so the hedge ratio comes out positive — [(€3,424 − 0)/€84.63] × 0.619489 = +25.06 — and the 25 contracts are bought. A short futures position would reduce the portfolio's basis point value instead of raising it toward the target.
rationales.C: 417 contracts is what the 9.5 target duration gives when it is applied to the €60,000,000 of bunds already held: 9.5 × 0.0001 × €60,000,000 = €57,000, and [(€57,000 − 0)/€84.63] × 0.619489 = 417.2. The existing holding already carries its own duration and needs no hedge; the target basis point value applies only to the €3,604,000 of new exposure the futures are being used to create, so BPVT = 9.5 × 0.0001 × €3,604,000 = €3,424 and the trade is about 25 contracts, not 417.

questions.stem: A manager uses futures and swaps to change a portfolio's equity and interest rate exposures over a short horizon instead of trading the underlying securities. Regarding these derivatives overlays, the most accurate statement is that:

options.A: they must be funded by selling underlying holdings.
options.B: they eliminate tracking risk relative to physical rebalancing.
options.C: they change exposures without disturbing underlying holdings.

rationales.A: Futures margin is a small fraction of the notional value controlled and is normally met out of cash reserves the portfolio already holds, so nothing has to be liquidated to post it. Not selling is the whole point of the overlay: the tax basis of the existing positions is preserved, no gains are realized, and voting rights are retained because no ownership is transferred.
rationales.B: An overlay narrows the gap to the target allocation, but it does not remove tracking risk. Contracts trade in whole units, so the notional rounds — 123.57 contracts becomes 124 — betas and modified durations are estimates that drift, the cheapest-to-deliver bond and conversion factor can change, and rolling positions costs money. Basis risk between the derivative and the exposure it stands in for therefore remains. The advantages of the overlay are speed, lower cost and leaving the holdings undisturbed, not the elimination of tracking risk.
rationales.C: Futures and swaps take targeted equity and interest rate risk exposures without disturbing the underlying holdings, and the benefits follow from that single feature: the tax basis of existing positions is preserved because no gains are realized, voting rights are kept because no ownership is transferred, the transaction costs of physically rebalancing a large book are avoided, the desired exposures are reached quickly and efficiently, and the positions can be reversed relatively easily when the view changes. Rossi uses futures for precisely this reason when he wants to shift €500 million of allocations over three months, and TMM executes a series of swaps that let it change its position temporarily but more easily and less expensively than by executing the physical transactions.

questions.stem: A manager wants to raise its large-cap and small-cap equity allocations and cut its government and corporate bond allocations without trading the underlying securities. Implemented with total return swaps, the allocation change most likely:

options.A: cannot be replicated in this way.
options.B: requires a single swap on one broad index.
options.C: requires several swaps on the sector indexes involved.

rationales.A: Replicating an allocation change is exactly what a total return swap does. The manager receives the total return of the index whose weight it wants to raise and pays the total return of the index whose weight it wants to cut, against floating payments tied to the market reference rate (MRR) minus an agreed-on spread, and the allocation moves without any security changing hands. TMM does this rather than trade stocks and bonds because the swaps change its position temporarily, more easily and less expensively than the physical transactions would.
rationales.B: The structure takes several legs, not one. TMM receives the total return of the S&P 500 to raise its large-cap weight and the total return of the S&P SmallCap 600 Index (SPSC) to raise its small-cap weight, while paying away the total return of the Bloomberg Barclays US Treasury Index (BBT) for the government bond sector and of the BofA Merrill Lynch US Corporate Index (BAMLC) for the corporate sector. One swap on one broad index cannot move four sector allocations in two different directions, and it would leave the manager with index exposure it did not ask for.
rationales.C: TMM raises the large-cap allocation by taking the return of the S&P 500 Index and the small-cap allocation by taking the return of the S&P SmallCap 600 Index (SPSC), and reduces the overall fixed-income allocation by replicating the Bloomberg Barclays US Treasury Index (BBT) for the government bond sector and the BofA Merrill Lynch US Corporate Index (BAMLC) for the corporate bond sector. On the equity leg, TMM receives the total return of the S&P 500 and makes a floating payment tied to the market reference rate (MRR) minus an agreed-on spread, both on a notional principal of $27 million. On the fixed-income leg, it pays the total return of the BBT and receives floating payments tied to MRR minus the agreed-on spread, both on a notional principal of $25 million. One swap per sector index, in the appropriate direction, is what reproduces the reallocation.

questions.stem: A manager replicates a change in asset allocation with total return swaps on broad equity and bond indexes while keeping its actively managed stock and bond portfolios in place. Regarding this transaction, the most accurate statement is that it:

options.A: is limited only by exchange margin requirements.
options.B: tracks imperfectly unless the portfolios are indexed to the swap indexes.
options.C: replicates the portfolios perfectly however they are constructed.

rationales.A: These are over-the-counter swaps, so there is no exchange margin to post; collateral is governed by the agreement between the counterparties. The limitations that matter are different ones: the swap pays the index return, not the portfolio's return, so a mismatch remains unless the portfolios are indexed to those same indexes, and the net cash flows have to be funded.
rationales.B: The transaction will not perfectly replicate the performance of the manager's equity and fixed-income portfolios unless those portfolios are indexed to the indexes selected as the underlying of the swaps; an actively managed book earns its own return while the swap pays the index return, and the difference is left with the manager. There is a second limitation alongside it: a cash flow problem arises if the fixed-income payments owed exceed the equity returns received and the portfolio does not generate enough cash to fund the net obligation. A stock and bond portfolio generates cash only from dividends and interest, because capital gains are not received in cash unless a portion of the portfolio is sold — and avoiding exactly that sale is the reason the manager wanted to use swaps in the first place.
rationales.C: Perfect replication requires the underlying portfolios to be indexed to the indexes used as the underlying of the swaps. An actively managed portfolio departs from its index by construction, so the swap return and the portfolio return diverge and a tracking gap remains however the swaps are sized.

questions.stem: A manager of an index-tracking equity fund is holding cash reserves and has no expectation about the direction of the underlying market over the next quarter, so she takes index futures positions against the cash. This cash equitization strategy is most likely intended to:

options.A: minimize tracking error against the benchmark.
options.B: add leverage beyond the benchmark exposure.
options.C: increase tracking error against the benchmark.

rationales.A: Cash equitization is used to minimize tracking error risk. A manager with no expectation about the direction of the underlying market implements it to replicate the performance of the relevant index on the cash reserves, so that idle cash earns the index return rather than dragging the fund below its benchmark. McMillian has no view on UK stocks over the next quarter but is keen to minimize tracking error risk, so she equitizes the cash reserves against the FTSE 100 and accomplishes that goal. Comparing the outcomes with and without the strategy shows the difference the overlay makes: a 5% return with it against 4.6% without it.
rationales.B: The strategy equitizes cash the fund already holds so that its market exposure matches the benchmark's, which removes cash drag rather than adding exposure on top of the benchmark. The futures notional is sized to the cash balance, not beyond it, so the fund's beta moves toward 1.0 against the index rather than above it.
rationales.C: The purpose runs the other way: replicating index performance on otherwise idle cash reduces the deviation between fund and benchmark returns. Leaving the cash unequitized is what increases tracking error, because the cash earns a money market return while the benchmark earns the index return.

questions.stem: A manager has used a one-year total return swap to shift its asset allocation and now wants out of the position before the swap matures. The position most likely:

options.A: cannot be exited before maturity.
options.B: can be offset with a new swap carrying opposite payments.
options.C: can be exited only by delivering the underlying index constituents.

rationales.A: Leaving a swap early is routine. The manager either negotiates a termination with the counterparty for the mark-to-market value or writes an offsetting swap, so the one-year term sets the horizon of the exposure rather than locking the manager in for it.
rationales.B: TMM could decide to unwind the position before one year elapses, which it could do by executing a new swap with opposite payments for the remainder of the life of the original swap: the two sets of payments cancel and the net exposure goes to zero. The same flexibility works the other way — if TMM wishes to extend the period, it would need to renegotiate the swap at expiration. That ability to reverse or extend as market conditions change is part of why the allocation shift was done with swaps rather than by trading the securities.
rationales.C: No physical delivery is involved. A total return swap settles the index's total return in cash against a floating payment, and the manager never owns the constituents, so there is nothing to deliver. The exit is a new swap with opposite payments for the remaining term, or a negotiated termination.

drills.los_text: demonstrate the use of derivatives in asset allocation, rebalancing, and inferring market expectations

questions.stem: Swaps, forwards and futures are written on interest rates, currencies, equities, bonds and volatility, and a manager can hold them long or short. Their common uses in portfolio management most likely include:

options.A: short-term speculation on price direction only.
options.B: no role in modern portfolio management.
options.C: modifying risk exposures, creating payoffs, rebalancing and inferring market expectations.

rationales.A: Directional bets are one corner of the map and not the largest. Alongside them sit hedging, creating payoff profiles that cash instruments cannot produce on their own, asset allocation and rebalancing, and reading market expectations out of derivative prices — uses that have nothing to do with taking a short-term view on direction.
rationales.B: These are core implementation tools rather than a sideshow. A manager who wants to change equity beta or portfolio duration, rebalance a drifted allocation, replicate a sector allocation, equitize cash or hedge a currency exposure reaches for them first, because they do the job faster and more cheaply than trading the underlying securities and leave the holdings undisturbed.
rationales.C: Four uses account for most of the activity, each with its own typical instruments. Modifying portfolio returns and risk exposures, whether for hedging or for directional bets, uses interest rate, currency and equity swaps and futures, fixed-income futures and variance swaps. Creating desired payoffs uses forwards, futures and total return swaps. Performing asset allocation and portfolio rebalancing uses equity index futures, government bond futures and index swaps. Inferring market expectations for interest rates, inflation and volatility uses Fed funds futures, inflation swaps and VIX futures.

questions.stem: Grant's portfolio has risen from €100 million to €106 million over the last month and now holds €46 million of European stocks and €60 million of German bunds. Restoring her target allocation requires cutting the equity exposure to €42.4 million. Regarding that target and the rebalancing she needs, the most accurate statement is that:

options.A: the target allocation is weighted more to bonds than to stocks.
options.B: restoring the target requires trading the underlying stocks and bonds.
options.C: the target allocation is weighted more to stocks than to bonds.

rationales.A: Grant manages the portfolio to a target allocation of 40% in stocks and 60% in bonds, so bonds carry the larger weight. Growth from €100 million to €106 million has left €46 million in European stocks, a beta of 1.2 with respect to the EURO STOXX 50 Index, and €60 million in German bunds with a modified duration of 9.5 — 43.4% and 56.6% of the portfolio against the 40% and 60% targets, or €42.4 million and €63.6 million in money terms. Grant will use stock index futures and bond futures to get back to those weights: once the notional values to be traded are known, she determines how many futures contracts should be bought or sold to achieve the desired asset allocation.
rationales.B: Grant rebalances with stock index futures and bond futures, which reset the equity and duration exposures without trading the underlying securities at all. That is the reason for using them: the holdings stay in place, their tax basis is preserved, and the transaction costs of selling €3.6 million of stocks and buying the same amount of bunds are avoided.
rationales.C: The weights are the wrong way round. Grant's target is 40% in stocks and 60% in bonds, not 60% in stocks and 40% in bonds, which is why the €46 million equity position — 43.4% of the €106 million portfolio — is above target and has to be reduced to €42.4 million rather than increased.

questions.stem: Inference of expected Federal Reserve policy moves at upcoming FOMC meetings is most likely based on the prices of:

options.A: equity index dividend futures.
options.B: fed funds futures contracts.
options.C: no traded instrument.

rationales.A: Equity index dividend futures price expected equity payout streams, not the path of policy rates. They carry no direct information about the FOMC's target range for the federal funds rate.
rationales.B: The commonly followed metric is the probability of a change in the federal funds rate at upcoming FOMC meetings that is implied by the prices of fed funds futures contracts. When the US central bank began its rate hiking cycle in 2015, it declared an intention to maintain a 25 bp target range (a lower and an upper bound) for the federal funds rate. The Fed regularly communicates its forward guidance along with the so-called dot plot, which shows where each FOMC meeting participant believes the federal funds rate should be at the end of the year, for the next few years, and in the longer run. The probabilities implied by fed funds futures prices represent the market's view and may diverge from that guidance.
rationales.C: Fed funds futures are the canonical instrument for this inference: the contract price is quoted off the market's expected effective federal funds rate, so prices translate directly into implied probabilities of rate changes at upcoming meetings.

questions.stem: The price of a fed funds futures contract is most likely quoted as the market's expectation for the effective federal funds (FFE) rate:

options.A: subtracted from 100.
options.B: added to 100.
options.C: less 100.

rationales.A: Fed funds futures are traded on the Chicago Board of Trade, and the contract price is quoted as 100 minus the market's expectation for the FFE rate: Fed funds futures contract price = 100 - Expected FFE rate. At expiration, the contract is cash settled to the simple average (overnight) effective federal funds rate for the delivery month, which is calculated and reported daily by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The underlying assumption is that implied futures market rates are predicting the monthly average effective federal funds rate.
rationales.B: Adding the expected rate to 100 would put the contract above par and make the price rise as expected rates rise. The quote is 100 minus the market's expected effective federal funds rate, so a 2% expectation implies a price of 98 and the price falls as expected rates rise.
rationales.C: This inverts the quote. The price is 100 minus the expected effective rate, not the expected rate minus 100, so a 2% expectation implies a price of 98, not -98.

questions.stem: The probability of an FOMC rate hike implied by fed funds futures is most likely calculated from:

options.A: the implied rate's position within the current-to-post-hike range.
options.B: the implied rate multiplied by the post-hike rate.
options.C: the current rate divided by the implied rate.

rationales.A: P(hike) = (Effective federal funds rate implied by the futures contract - Current federal funds rate) / (Federal funds rate assuming a rate hike - Current federal funds rate), where the current federal funds rate is the midpoint of the current target range and the post-hike rate is the midpoint of the range that would follow the hike. The implied rate's position within that interval is the probability the market attaches to the move.
rationales.B: A product of two interest rate levels has no probability interpretation and is not bounded by 0 and 1. The calculation interpolates instead: (implied FFE rate - current federal funds rate) / (post-hike federal funds rate - current federal funds rate).
rationales.C: A simple ratio of two rate levels carries no probability content. It ignores the size of the Fed's declared incremental move, which supplies the denominator of the interpolation (post-hike rate - current rate), and it would not be bounded by 0 and 1.

questions.stem: A fed funds futures contract expiring after the next FOMC meeting is priced at 97.90, and the current federal funds rate target range is set between 1.75% and 2.00%. The effective federal funds (FFE) rate implied by the futures price is closest to:

rationales.A: The FFE rate implied by the futures contract price is 2.10% (= 100 - 97.90). The midpoint of the current 1.75%-2.00% target range is 1.875%, and given the Fed's declared incremental move size of 25 bps, a hike would produce a new target range of 2.00%-2.25% with a midpoint of 2.125%. The probability of a hike is therefore (2.100% - 1.875%)/(2.125% - 1.875%) = 0.225/0.25 = 0.90, or 90%, a high probability that the FOMC will increase rates by 25 bps.
rationales.B: The quote convention is inverted here. The implied FFE rate is 100 minus the futures price, 100 - 97.90 = 2.10%, a positive rate, not the price minus 100.
rationales.C: 1.875% is the midpoint of the current target range (1.75%-2.00%), which serves as the base rate later in the probability calculation rather than as the futures-implied rate. The implied FFE rate comes from the contract price: 100 - 97.90 = 2.10%.

questions.stem: Typical end-of-month (EOM) activity by large banks lifts the relevant fed funds futures price to 98.05. The current federal funds target range is 1.75%–2.00% (midpoint 1.875%), and the Fed moves in 25 bp increments. The implied probability of a rate hike is closest to:

rationales.A: The interpolation gives (1.950% - 1.875%)/0.25% = 0.30, not 0.60. No step in the calculation produces 0.60.
rationales.B: 0.90 is the probability before the end-of-month dip, when the futures price was 97.90 and the implied effective rate 2.10%. The lower implied rate of 1.95% cuts the probability to 0.30.
rationales.C: Typical end-of-month (EOM) activity by large financial and banking institutions often induces dips in the FFE rate that create bias issues when the rate is used as the basis for probability calculations of potential FOMC rate moves. With such activity lifting the price of the relevant fed funds futures contract to 98.05, the FFE rate declines to 1.95% (= 100 - 98.05). Using the same equation as before, the probability of an FOMC rate hike decreases from 90% to just 30%: (1.950 - 1.875)/0.25 = 0.30, or 30%. To overcome this end-of-month bias, data providers have implemented various methods of smoothing the EOM dips.

questions.stem: Correcting fed funds futures-implied probabilities for end-of-month dips in the effective federal funds rate most likely involves:

options.A: a forward rate structure built from non-FOMC meeting months.
options.B: survey-based expectations in place of futures data.
options.C: no available correction.

rationales.A: One prominent data provider uses a method that builds a forward rate structure based on where the market believes interest rates will settle in non-FOMC meeting months and then uses these forward rates to make appropriate adjustments. For each FOMC meeting month, it is assumed that an effective rate prevails until the meeting date and then some other rate prevails after the meeting, with the average effective rate over the month being implied by the futures price.
rationales.B: Futures prices remain the input. The method builds a forward rate structure from where the market expects rates to settle in months without an FOMC meeting and uses those forward rates to adjust the meeting-month rate, smoothing the end-of-month artifacts rather than replacing market pricing with survey expectations.
rationales.C: The end-of-month dips are a recognized bias and are corrected. A prominent data provider's smoothing method addresses exactly this bias, building forward rates from non-FOMC meeting months and adjusting the meeting-month assumption accordingly.

questions.stem: Policy rate probabilities implied by fed funds futures prices are most likely to:

options.A: diverge from the Fed's forward guidance.
options.B: coincide with the Fed's forward guidance.
options.C: foretell the actual policy rate path.

rationales.A: Implied market expectations can diverge significantly from the Fed's forward guidance. Such implied probabilities represent the market's view and may diverge from the guidance provided by central banks in their regular communications about the likely future course of monetary policy actions, including the dot plot that shows where each FOMC meeting participant believes the federal funds rate should be at the end of the year, for the next few years, and in the longer run. The forward guidance line is the median of those dots, and the implied-expectations line can sit well away from it.
rationales.B: Guidance and market pricing come from different parties and routinely differ. Implied probabilities represent the market's view and can diverge significantly from central bank guidance, especially over longer horizons.
rationales.C: These are current expectations, and especially for the longer-term horizon the inferred probabilities usually do not have strong predictive power. They neither match guidance nor foretell actual outcomes.

questions.stem: Probabilities inferred from derivatives prices are best described as:

options.A: current expectations that new information can change.
options.B: reliable forecasts of actual central bank decisions.
options.C: noise without informational content.

rationales.A: It is important to emphasize that these inferences relate to current expectations of future events - they do not foretell what will actually happen - which can change with the arrival of new information. They are useful for gauging market sentiment and priced-in expectations, but not for predicting actual outcomes with certainty.
rationales.B: They are current expectations, not predictions. Realized outcomes routinely diverge from the path priced in, and the inferred probabilities usually do not have strong predictive power, especially over longer horizons.
rationales.C: The information is real and closely watched, and implied probabilities are published and tracked over time by data providers. The caveat is its nature as a snapshot of expectations that shifts with new information, not an absence of content.

questions.stem: The implied probabilities of a hike, no change, and a cut at a particular FOMC meeting date are most likely:

options.A: greater than one in total when uncertainty is high.
options.B: unrelated to one another.
options.C: equal to one in total.

rationales.A: The outcome probabilities always sum to exactly one, whatever the level of uncertainty, because the three actions exhaust the possibilities. High uncertainty spreads the probability mass more evenly across hike, no change, and cut; it does not add to the total.
rationales.B: The three outcomes are jointly constrained. The probability of a hike and the probability of a cut, together with the probability of no change, complete the unit mass at that meeting date, so raising one necessarily lowers the others.
rationales.C: The probability of a rate hike or cut is represented as the probability of a move from the current target range at the specified meeting date, and the probabilities of all three actions - hike, no change, and cut - at a particular meeting date sum to 1. Data providers show trends in these implied probabilities over time.

questions.stem: A $200 million portfolio enters a combination of equity and fixed-income swaps to move to a target allocation of 90% stocks and 10% bonds, taking long equity legs totaling $30 million against short fixed-income legs totaling $30 million. The allocation in place before the swaps is most likely:

options.A: 75% stocks, 25% bonds.
options.B: 25% stocks, 75% bonds.
options.C: 100% large-cap stocks.

rationales.A: The target equity allocation is 90% of $200 million, or $180 million. The swaps add $30 million of long equity exposure, so equity before the swaps was $180 million - $30 million = $150 million, which is 75% of the portfolio, leaving 25% ($50 million) in bonds. The long legs are $27 million in the S&P 500 (large cap moving from 60% to 65%) and $3 million in the S&P SmallCap 600 (10% unchanged), against short legs of $25 million in the government bond index and $5 million in the corporate bond index. The $45 million mid-cap exposure does not change, so no mid-cap index needs to be incorporated into the swap. The swap is structured so that all payments occur on the same dates six months apart and matures in one year; extending that period would require renegotiating the swap at expiration, and unwinding before one year elapses could be done by executing a new swap with opposite payments for the remainder of the original swap's life.
rationales.B: The weights are reversed. Starting from 25% equity, reaching a 90% equity target would require $130 million of new long equity exposure, not $30 million. Long legs of $30 million on a $200 million portfolio shift the equity weight by 15 percentage points, which places the starting weight at 75%.
rationales.C: An all-equity portfolio would already exceed the 90% equity target and would need no long equity legs at all, let alone short bond legs to fund them. The starting portfolio is a 75/25 stock/bond mix spanning large-, mid-, and small-cap equities together with government and corporate bonds, not solely large-cap stocks.
